news.title: 'Head on collision' with RTÉ and government looming as row erupts over €20 million budget cut
news.text: A row has reignited as RTÉ was dealt a blow with €20 million less funding than promised in Budget 2027, with the broadcaster's top boss threatening: "We now have some important decisions to make." Media Minister Patrick O’Donovan defended the allocation, saying he is "unhappy" with the public broadcaster’s reform since the 2023 Ryan Tubridy payment scandal . But RTÉ Director-General Kevin Bakhurst hit back at this claim , saying: "We completely reject the assertion that the pace of reform and transformation within RTÉ has been slow." Mr Bakhurst threatened that without this funding RTÉ’s five-year strategy transformation will be impacted. A governance and financial crisis was triggered at the broadcaster when it was revealed that it had underreported Tubridy’s earnings by €345,000 over four years. To help it rebuild, the government committed to providing a €725 million public funding bailout over three years. For 2027, RTÉ was due to be given €260 million of this. But Minister O’Donovan said a smaller sum of €240 million was allocated in Budget 2027 as it reflects the overall funding available in his department. This will be made up of €66 million in direct Exchequer support, and €174 million in projected licence fee collections. However, the Fine Gael minister hasn’t solely blamed the €20 million reduction on his department’s allocated budget package. He reignited a row with the broadcaster, accusing top bosses of failing to reform the public broadcaster in a timely manner. Speaking today, the Media Minister said: "While progress has been made across a number of issues, I am not happy that we have seen sufficient progress in delivering the smaller, more agile processes that we sought to be delivered under the strategy." RTÉ is now seeking a meeting with the minister over the funding. Mr Bakhurst rejected Minister O'Donovan's claims, saying his team has delivered “extensive reform” since he took on the role of director general in July 2023. In a statement, he added: "The clarity provided through this multi-annual funding agreement enabled RTÉ to plan ahead, to deliver trusted, independent news and analysis. "To commit to producing more public service programmes and content for audiences, including original Irish drama and live sport, to invest in podcasts, apps and the RTÉ Player, to implement a digital commercial strategy, to stabilise our finances, and to make good on our plans." The top boss criticised the government for reducing the public funding agreement three months before it is due to be given. He said: "The government’s decision to reduce this public funding agreement by €20 million at this late stage, when we have already made important commitments to our audiences, to the independent sector, to other important stakeholders and to RTÉ staff, is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy. "If the three-year multi-annual agreement will no longer be honoured – we now have some important decisions to make." Chair of the Oireachtas Media Committee Alan Kelly has demanded that Minister O'Donovan urgently explain the reason for cutting the agreed public funding by €20 million. He said this needs to be resolved "urgently" as a "head-on collision between RTÉ and government is now looming." news.title: Israelis gather to remember victims of October 7th attack
news.text:
Israelis gathered on Wednesday at some 400 protests across the country to mark the third anniversary of the October 7th, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. 

They renewed calls for a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the worst day in the country’s history, when 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage to Gaza. 

Israeli president Yitzhak Herzog launched the commemorations by lighting a memorial candle at the president’s residence at 6.29am, the time the Hamas attack started.

Herzog then travelled to Netiv HaAsara, a farming community on the Gaza border, where militants on hang gliders landed on October 7th at the start of the invasion.

Memorial services took place at kibbutzim and other communities along the Gaza border that bore the brunt of the Hamas onslaught after the border fence was breached at more than 100 separate locations in the first hour of the attack.

At noon on Wednesday, hundreds of thousands of people observed a moment of silence across the country. 

Protesters brought the burnt-out shells of cars belonging to victims of the Nova music festival massacre to the demonstration outside the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in Jerusalem.

Some 378 people were killed at the Nova site, the vast majority of them young revellers who were still dancing when the first rockets landed in the area. The rockets were followed minutes later by gunmen on motorcycles who opened fire indiscriminately. 

Provocative art installations were also a feature of Wednesday’s events. At Tel Aviv’s Dizengoff Square, protesters dyed the fountain water red. Rows of cut-out human figures were laid along a Tel Aviv beach, alongside a message reading: “October 7th – the price of the failure.”

Nine-month-old Kfir Bibas was the youngest victim of the Hamas attack. He died in captivity in Gaza along with his mother and elder brother, Ariel (4). His father Yarden, who was kidnapped separately and returned to Israel, issued a heartfelt message at the ceremony in kibbutz Nir Oz. “Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here.”

Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu lit a memorial candle honouring the October 7th victims, saying: “We will complete the mission. We came to settle the score with all the murderers, and we will.”

Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation.

A survey released on Wednesday found that most Israelis believe the goals set out by Netanyahu at the beginning of the war, described as “total victory”, have not been achieved. 

Fewer than 20 per cent believe these goals have been achieved to a large extent or in full. Fewer than half of respondents believe Israel is safer today than it was before October 7th, while nearly a third believe the country is not as safe. 

Israel’s bombardment and ground operations in Gaza ​since the October 7th attack have killed more than 74,000 people, including at least 1,400 killed in the past year since a US-brokered ceasefire, which halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks or ​secure the disarmament of Hamas.

news.summary: Thousands observed a moment of silence as Netanyahu promised to ‘complete the mission’
news.author: Mark Weiss

Financial adviser on Budget 2027 
 Is the Irish government finally growing up?

Yesterday’s budget showed a more mature approach to Ireland’s finances from the government, but it did also leave some of the country’s biggest problems untouched.

7.16pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Ralph Benson

IS OUR GOVERNMENT adulting? Our lookalike finance ministers (average age: 37) seem to have grown up. They have set out a budget which opens up opportunities for many people.

The government has moved beyond scattering €500 in every direction and hoping for the best, as witnessed in previous budgets. Instead, there is improved focus on some key areas that will build value for many years into the future.

Above all, there is a definite move towards a more mature culture of personal investing, saving, and wealth-building in this budget. As we’ll see, that’s important, because the government does not show much interest in building rainy day savings of its own. What’s also important is that this budget is less about creating winners and losers, and more about how each of us can take up the opportunities it offers, whatever our current financial position.

A budget for building wealth

There are three big positives for people trying to build wealth. First, the much-ballyhooed investment scheme. It turns out to be a touch more generous than many expected. You can add €12,000 a year, and you’re not taxed on the portion above €50,000. Above that, a 1% rate applies.

To be sure, there will be people who get a shock in a year they lose money and still find themselves paying the 1% wealth tax. But that is some time away – and many others will find a way to squirrel away, say, €24,000 over time, and double their money tax-free as investment markets do their work.

For many people, that’s a sizeable house deposit, or will fund children through third-level, or kill off the mortgage a few years early. It will also help spur a wider culture of investing, in a way the fabled SSIAs never did. We all knew they were too good to be repeated.

A positive aspect of this investment scheme is that you can start from low amounts. And it’ll be widely on offer from banks, brokers and online platforms. It seems likely that in five or seven years’ time, it’ll be as normal a part of our personal finances as opening credit union accounts and swapping Dunnes Stores money-off vouchers.

So much for the new. What about adjustments to existing arrangements? Much-despised taxes on investment returns have been cut, if not fully reformed. Capital gains tax falls from 33% to 31%, a move few expected. And exit tax on mutual funds falls from 38% to 35%, though fixing with Ireland’s weird deemed disposal regime is just too hard. Finance Minister Simon Harris has said that this “rule is something that we need to move beyond”. Just not yet, apparently.

Advertisement

Thirdly, there are the rising inheritance bands. Your son or daughter can now inherit €420,000 tax-free, taking €6,600 out of the tax net. Intergenerational wealth is a fairly new concept in Ireland, and this will help families looking to pass assets on – whether on death or as a gift in life.

So if you are serious about getting on in Ireland in 2027, there is quite a lot on offer. Here’s how three groups of grownups can take advantage:

When we were young

For those who are first-time adulting, a 15% increase in rent tax credit is useful, though the €5,000 rise in help-to-buy deposits will probably just filter through to sellers as these measures tend to. The government also seems serious about making childcare more affordable – but as with housing, shies away from measures that increase supply and fix underlying problems.

Personal investment accounts look quite attractive for younger adults. The fact that they reward risk, and pay no interest on cash will make them inappropriate for most house deposit savings.

But unlike pensions, the benefit of which is so far away, these accounts offer the prospect of building some decent money in a timeframe you can visualise.

Longer term, this group will benefit most from enormous investments into Dublin’s MetroLink, as well as the building up of Ireland’s sovereign wealth fund – the Future Ireland Fund – with a total €5.8 billion commitment, available for spending from 2041 onwards.

Card-carrying grown-ups will welcome a rise in the threshold at which top-rate tax is paid, even if it is a bit stingy. It’s moved from €44,000 to €46,500 for a single person – effectively a tax saving of €500 if you earn €46,500 or more. The risk here was a repeat of last year, where it didn’t move at all.

Fully-grown adults will also benefit from cuts to USC, to third-level costs, and a hike in the amount you can feed to the electricity grid from your solar panels, as well as inflation-based uplift in children’s allowance.

Lastly, if you’re trying to make more with less, there is also a certain amount for you. Rent-a-room relief now enables €16,000 of tax-free income a year – an 11% increase. Social welfare benefits have been moved up, and the main tax credits increased by €125.

Of course, there will always be demands for more. But what looks like generosity comes with trade-offs. For example, in accepting the Low Pay Commission’s recommendation to increase the minimum wage by 5.3% to €14.94, we risk hitting limits where businesses will be willing to employ young people entering the workforce for the first time.

What might have been

The trouble with grownups is they sometimes stay out too late enjoying themselves, when they should be attending to the serious stuff. There’s no doubt the budget misses several opportunities. These can be divided into three kinds:

Related Reads

Fine Gael canvassers get chilly reception from Dublin commuters ahead of price hikes

Where's the protest gone? No rows, no riots, and not even a 'hup ya boy ya'

Budget 2027: What changed at midnight - and what we'll have to wait for

Firstly, there’s the addiction to adding to our already complicated tax system, rather than taking things away. For example, here are some of the tax rates that now apply to investments, depending on where you keep your money in Ireland: 1% (personal investment accounts), 25% (companies), 31% (capital gains), 35% (exit tax next year), 38% (exit tax now). This has little logic behind it.

Then there’s the fact that we continue to depend so much on corporation tax receipts and the top end of income taxpayers. Here’s how the government’s own spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC), marked their homework: “Budget 2027 puts the public finances on a worse trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.

Ouch. In particular, IFAC points out, corporation tax receipts are volatile and dependent on a handful of US companies, yet the government is spending €6 out of every €7 that it gets. What’s the plan if that dries up? The risk is that the government will be forced to borrow more, at a time when the cost of government borrowing is on the rise.

Finally, there’s the lack of appetite for the real reform on the big problems that dog life in Ireland in 2026. Our government has little to say when it comes to the hard work of fixing the planning, supply and cost control issues that would sort causes rather than symptoms, and help deal with the housing backlog, slow infrastructure delivery and missing football pitches people could really do with.

Instead, we continue to throwing subsidies at housing, childcare, transport and other vocal constituencies. There is no real attempt to control costs. We’ve found a whopping €6 billion of additional cash for MetroLink! That’s €6 million extra per working day, yet is barely noticed compared to much less consequential tweaks.

These missed opportunities at government level are exactly why it’s vital for individuals to make the most of what’s available in Budget 2027. Make sure you take the opportunity.

Ralph Benson is a chartered accountant and head of financial advice at online investments and pensions adviser at Moneycube.ie.

news.title: Jon Rahm to end LIV Golf involvement due to ‘unacceptable terms’ on offer
news.text:
Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf due to the “unacceptable” terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series.

LIV is currently going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the United States after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund withdrew support at the end of the season having spent $5 billion (€4.46 billion) in four years.

While the likes of Sergio Garcia were successful in petitioning the court to lift the automatic stay on their contracts, effectively freeing them up to pursue other opportunities next year, Rahm was not afforded the same escape.

The Spaniard is one of the two big LIV names – Bryson DeChambeau the other – and is reported to be owed up to $150 million (€134 million) for the remainder of the contract he signed almost three years ago.

“Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 ... and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” attorney John Beck told a bankruptcy hearing.

The Athletic also reported Beck told the court Rahm and LIV are working to finalise a separation agreement by October 15th.

Rahm withdrew from this week’s Open de Espana in Madrid in order to remain at home as wife Kelley is expecting their fourth child.

In May, the 31-year-old backed down in his dispute with the DP World Tour and paid around €2.6 million in fines for playing in competing events, giving him conditional releases for 2026 and making him eligible for the Ryder Cup.

He previously opted not to take the PGA Tour’s offer of reinstatement via a specially drawn-up Returning Member Program created in January and applicable to only him, Cam Smith, Bryson DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka – the only player who accepted the offer.

As a result, Rahm would have to serve a mandatory one-year suspension, up until late August next year, before he could return to the American circuit.

ColumnDig Your Heels In

Lise Hand: I'm mourning the era of high heels (but I don't think I'd go back all the same)

Gone are the days when heels were an absolute necessity for days in the office and nights on the town.

7.01pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

ABOUT 5PM LAST Friday evening in Dublin city, just as people high-tailed it from workplaces to head for the hills, the bus, tram, train, the M50 (thoughts and prayers) or to the pub, the skies opened with a biblical vengeance. It rained cats, dogs, pitchforks; it came down like stair rods; it bucketed, lashed, hammered down.

Scurrying down a rapidly emptying side street, a sudden loud racket close by caused this writer’s heart to briefly depart her carcass; a few seconds later a cavalcade of half-soaked young women tottered past, swearing and half-drowned.

It wasn’t the fusillade of swearing which induced the jump-scare though – instead it was the noisy blast of fast-moving stilettos clattering along the pavement, a percussive, staccato rat-tat on concrete.

The women were clearly dressed for going out-out. But while they were perfectly en vogue from the ankles up, a parade of slip dresses and cropped faux fur jackets, their unanimous choice of footwear seemed oddly anachronistic, as if they had just stepped (carefully) out of a Tardis after a round trip to the 1990s.

They were sporting proper high heels.

The standing-on-tippy-toe type which basically requires balancing atop a three or four-inch nail – and not just balancing, mind, but also performing other feats of equipoise such as walking, dancing, standing around for hours and running for a bus.

In other words, the type of shoe which was the automatic accessory of choice or of necessity for at least a couple of generations of women.

The disappearance of heels from office life started with wearing flats for the commute, then grew to switching over altogether.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Until, thank God, it wasn’t. The quasi-extinction of the high-heeled shoe has been as swift as it has been welcome. True, there are still various degrees of slightly elevated footwear out and about to be sure, such as block heels, wedges and kitten heels, but even they’re lesser-spotted objects these days, easily spotted among the forest of flatties.

Advertisement

Heels had a hold over us

Why the hell did we do the high heel thing for so long? Because we bought into the canny propaganda, is the short answer. First and foremost, the stiletto has been long touted as a signifier of feminine sexiness. Think of the iconic scene in the 1950s Hollywood classic ‘Some Like it Hot’ when Tony Curtis and Jack Lemon, gussied up like a pair of dames, goggle at how a stiletto-wearing Marilyn Monroe sashays with ease along a train platform. “Look at that! Look how she moves! That’s just like Jell-O on springs… must have some sort of built-in motor or something,” marvels Lemon.

Then in more recent decades, in an effort to recast the high heel as a feminist statement, spiky heels and a shoulder-padded suit came to signify a ball-breaking boardroom badass high-kicking her way through corporate glass ceilings. In 2012, Victoria Beckham, who by now had remarkably transmogrified from the Spice Girl who pointed rather than sang into the designer darling of New York fashion week, explained her adherence to vertiginous heels. “I can’t concentrate in flats,” she told a TV interviewer.

It was pure Carrie Bradshaw-speak.

If any one figure promoted the high heel as simultaneously an implement of enticement, a girl’s best friend and an ambitious woman’s weapon of choice, it was the Manolo Blahnik-obsessed character played by Sarah Jessica Parker in HBO’s massive hit series Sex and the City who regularly uttered empowering nuggets such as: “The fact is, sometimes it’s hard to walk in a single woman’s shoes. That’s why we need really special ones now and then – to make the walk a little more fun.” Or: “Maybe the reason Cinderella was so happy wasn’t because of the Prince…. but because of the shoes.”

Sarah Jessica Parker's iconic character was well known for her love of shoes.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Sex and the City had perfect timing, coinciding with the boomiest of boom times at the tail-end of the 1990s and the early 2000s, when oodles of money was flying around like snuff at a wake and when the phrase “girl power” made it into the Oxford English Dictionary. However, it’s no coincidence that by the time the second full-length spin-off movie was released in 2010, the economic and societal mood had darkened considerably, and the film was universally kicked to flitters by critics for its tone-deaf materialism and naff consumerism.

Coming back down to earth

Heels, like hemlines, rise in optimistic times, and lower when the outlook is less sunny.

The descent of high heels started slowly; women took to wearing tights and trainers on their commute to work, before slipping into a heeled court shoe (nude-coloured being the ‘colour’ of choice) outside the entrance or as soon as they reached their desk. It wouldn’t do at all to be caught literally flat-footed in the workplace.

Thankfully, once a dazed workforce had emerged from the smoking rubble of the global financial crash of the late naughties, this pointless ritual had largely bitten the dust. Trainers, high-tops, Doc Martens, ballet pumps, biker boots, loafers and brogues pounded pavements and adorned the feet of front row fashionistas from Manhattan to Milan.

The Covid pandemic finally did for the office high heel – the notion of clacking about in any sort of shoe, tight skirt or even an underwired bra for that matter while working from home was ludicrous – sales of high heels reportedly dropped by 65% during the second quarter of 2020, according to market research data.

Interestingly, once the pandemic receded, the stiletto failed to make a triumphant comeback, despite the imprecations and predictions of various glossy magazines.

It turns out that unlike many fashion accessories, flats weren’t just a fad – they represented a redrawing of how women move through the world.

Related Reads

Lise Hand: Hilda Moriarty inspired ‘Raglan Road’, so why isn't she remembered?

Lise Hand: Swear to God, I saw U2 play in the Dandelion Market too 

‘Killer heels’ are no longer status symbols among women who want to be able to run unimpeded and in comfort for a bus or from a creepy stalker or for public office. Even the world of haute couture copped on. “The flat shoe makes the woman equal to men. When they have high (shoes) they play a part like a geisha, and they can’t be expected to be taken that seriously,” observed designer Karl Lagerfeld.

Flat shoes and short heels are back in style.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Therefore it’s unsurprising that one place where high-heeled women are most conspicuous is anywhere in the near vicinity of that doughty defender of gender equality, Donald Trump. MAGA’s botoxed, trout-lipped, stilettoed chattels totter around Mar-a-Lago and the White House, mostly pound shop versions of Melania Trump who is usually spotted perched atop spindly Louboutin stilettos during her rare tight-lipped forays into public with her husband. But wherever they all go, any glass ceilings above them remain unbothered and intact.

However, back in rainy Dublin, I watched the tangle of leggy women scurrying for shelter, and felt a pang for my most beloved-ever shoes, a long-departed pair of sleek, pointy-toed caramel-coloured buttery-leather Prada stilettos which looked sexy as hell, yet which felt like wearing fluffy slippers. They were miraculous, and I mourned them when they were consigned to the bin, finally beyond repair. I’ve never felt similar fierce affection for any pair of trainers or Chelsea boots, to be honest. Flatties are, well, grand.

There’s nothing wrong with sallying forth in a pair of towering stilettos when the occasion, the mood or the outfit calls for it. Sometimes, being Jell-O on springs feels damn fine.

But now it’s a choice, not a duty. And that’s the whole pointy-pointe of it.

Lise Hand is a journalist and writer. This column runs every Wednesday.

news.title: Helen McEntee admits end of peacekeeping mission in Lebanon will likely lead to exodus from Defence Forces
news.text:
Public expenditure minister Jack Chambers told the Dáil during Budget 2027 speeches that funding would provide for an intake of 850 new permanent Defence Forces members.

This will provide for 400 brand new personnel members, with 450 other roles filled due to departures of existing staff members.

Ms McEntee conceded that reaching the target of 11,500 troops by the end of 2028 is “not likely”, with the force expected to reach 8,300 by the end of 2028.

The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) mission will finish by the end of the year following the failure of the United Nations Security Council to renew its mandate.

Ireland cannot partake in missions without a UN mandate under the current Triple Lock legislation.

Ms McEntee said that once the Unifil mission is wound down by Easter, the number of defence personnel overseas will fall from over 400 to 90, with those members working in office roles.

The minister contended that the number of Defence Forces personnel is likely to fall once the Lebanon mission wraps up.

“When we talk about recruitment and retention, I had the opportunity to meet with those who were the last battalion that went out to Lebanon," she said. 

"When I spoke to many of them, they joined because they wanted to come to Lebanon. They joined because they wanted to serve in overseas peacekeeping missions.

“If we do not have those opportunities for people, I believe that that will impact on those who wish to join but also retaining people who are actually in the permanent Defence Forces.”

She said that she does not believe that there will be a new UN-mandated mission to Lebanon, but talks are underway for an EU Common Security and Defence Policy mission to be deployed to Lebanon once UNIFIL comes to an end.

However, she said Ireland will not be able to join this while the Triple Lock is still in place.

 Louise Burne is Political Correspondent.
news.summary: The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) mission will finish by the end of the year following the failure of the United Nations Security Council to renew its mandate
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Louise Burne

news.title: Call for safer access to Simon’s Cove near Clonakilty
news.text:
Safety concerns over access to Simon’s Cove, a pretty secluded cove near Clonakilty popular with swimmers, have been raised by West Cork councillors.

Independent Ireland councillor Daniel Sexton said the cliff route down to the water needed to be examined as an increasing number of people visit the location. 

He told a meeting of Cork County Council’s Western Division that the cove was a beautiful spot, but access was a concern.

Mr Sexton said swimmers and other visitors were making their way down to the water and that the council needed to consider whether anything could be done to make the approach safer.

He raised the issue following an update on coastal and marine projects across West Cork.

Fine Gael councillor John Michael Foley also raised concerns about coastal access and safety at Broadstrand. 

A council official said the Simon’s Cove matter had been raised at an earlier local meeting and would be examined. 

The official said the council would investigate the position at the site and consider what options, if any, were available. No works programme, cost estimate, or timeline was given.

The discussion took place as the council outlined ongoing work on coastal protection, harbour infrastructure, and public access at sites across West Cork. 

Its coastal projects report includes monitoring work at vulnerable beaches and coastal locations, where sand movement, erosion, and changing conditions can affect access and existing defences. 

The council said it would revert to councillors once it had examined the Simon’s Cove concern.

 Funded by the Local Democracy Reporting Scheme
news.summary: A councillor John Michael Foley also raised concerns at Cork County Council’s Western Division about coastal access and safety at Broadstrand
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,West Cork

news.title: ‘We need the truth’: Calls for public inquiry into Creeslough tragedy on fourth anniversary
news.text:
Hundreds of people, including the families of those who died in the Creeslough explosion of October 7th, 2022, gathered at the site of the tragedy on Wednesday to remember their loved ones four years on.

Ten people, ranging in age from five to 59, died in the blast. Robert Garwe and his daughter Shauna Flanagan-Garwe (5), Catherine O’Donnell and her son James Monaghan (13), Jessica Gallagher, Martin McGill, James O’Flaherty, Martina Martin, Hugh Kelly and Leona Harper (14) were all killed in the explosion.

Heavy rain gave way to bright sunshine at the scene of the tragedy, as prayers were said for lost loved ones.

At the stroke of 3.17pm, at the exact moment of the explosion, an eerie silence fell over the village.

Some family members who lost loved ones in the tragedy spoke after the short service.

Áine Flanagan, who lost her partner Robert and daughter Shauna in the blast, said that the families were now entering a fifth year without their loved ones.

She said it was “heartbreaking”, and all they wanted was the truth of what happened on that Friday afternoon in October 2022.

“We, the families, we deserve answers,” she said.

When asked what life was like without her partner and daughter, she replied, “It’s painful. I’m missing them every day.”

Donna Harper, whose daughter Leona was just 14 when she was killed in the explosion after entering the garage for an ice-cream, said the pain simply never gets any easier.

She said: “We’re standing here four years on, and it never gets any easier. I still miss my wee girl every single day, every moment of every day.”

“I stood here for almost 24 hours, across the road, waiting for my wee girl to be found, hoping and praying for a miracle that she would be brought out. That didn’t happen, and my wee girl never came home.”

She added that unless the families get the truth of what caused the explosion, they will never be able to move on.

“We need answers, we need to know what happened, why it happened, how it happened. We need to know the truth to be able to move on,” she said.

Her husband, Hugh, said he still recalls waiting at “this very spot” for his daughter’s remains to be taken out from the scene of the carnage.

However, he says it’s wrong to say that his only daughter is not with her family still.

Choking back tears, he said: “She is here. She’s with me. She’s there in the morning, she’s there at night ... first and last thoughts.

“But life is not the same. It’s changed.

“It’s just hard to put it into words, it really is, but the loss, it can’t be measured. It just can’t be measured,” he added.

He said he had one simple request for the Government – to never allow something like this to happen again to any other family.

“I just wish that the Government would come on board, that they would establish a public inquiry for the simple reason as to examine every possible avenue of how this was allowed to happen, and not let it happen again.”

Fr John Joe Duffy read out the names of the victims in the order that they were pronounced dead at the time of the tragedy at the service.

The families were joined in solidarity by members of the Stardust Victims’ Committee as well as members of the Bloody Sunday Trust.

Fr Duffy appealed to everyone gathered to support each other on their journey of healing.

He said: “As we gather here today, as we stand here in this place today, grief does not end, and everyone, while on a collective journey, is at a different stage on the road towards healing.

“Some may have started that journey, while others have found that they have not yet been able to even begin on that journey to healing.”

Members of the emergency services who attended the scene on the day were also present, as well as senior gardaí and a number of elected members of Donegal County Council.
news.summary: Áine Flanagan, who lost her partner Robert and daughter Shauna in the blast, said families ‘deserve answers’
news.author: Stephen Maguire

Defence Forces will not reach target of 11,500 personnel by 2028 despite recruitment commitments

Defence Minister Helen McEntee was speaking at a press conference about the Defence and Foreign Affairs allocations in Budget 2027.

6.41pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Niall O'Connor

THE MINISTER FOR Defence has said the Irish Defence Forces will not reach 11,500 troops by 2028, breaking a key target promised by the organisation and government. 

The Commission on the Defence Forces report set a target of 11,500 as a critical part of its plan to meet what has been defined as Level of Ambition Two in the military regeneration. 

This was committed to by the government and the Defence Forces, but now Helen McEntee has said she accepts that will not be achieved.

McEntee was speaking at a press conference about Budget 2027 and the Defence and Foreign Affairs allocations. 

When asked if she believed recruitment targets would be met, she accepted that they would not be. 

“It’s a very difficult task at this stage,” she said. 

“However, what is very clear, in particular in the last two years, is that the trajectory for recruits is going in the right direction. So we’re recruiting more, we’re retaining more importantly, and there’s more people applying every year.

“So we’ve increased by 790 last year, to 850 I hope this year, and 900 the year after. So if we can continue in that vein,” she added. 

Advertisement

The minister also spoke about her hopes of increased civilianisation in the Defence Forces with 100 civil servants due to be recruited. McEntee explained that such a move has worked in An Garda Síochána, and she believes it will be of benefit to the military also. 

In the budget there was €340 million in National Development Plan funding. The minister said that this will cover the cost of the Primary Radar Project, which was confirmed in recent weeks. 

This would see Ireland’s first air defence systems and radar around the island to monitor the airspace and detect rogue aircraft that civilian services cannot see. 

In February the Department of Defence announced the purchase of armoured personnel carriers to replace the ageing MOWAG fleet after an agreement with the French government.

Sources have said that this could cost more than €600m, with some suggesting it may be as expensive as €900m due to the ever-increasing level of defence inflation in the cost of equipment. 

However, there was no mention of this in the budget. McEntee said that there would be “budgets beyond next year to fund our armoured vehicles”. She explained that she was looking for an increase in 2028 in the NDP provision for Defence.

The minister said she was open to exploring the EU’s SAFE defence loans – this is a money pot developed by Brussels to give long term loans of 30 to 40 years in duration.

“I would like us to be part of SAFE. I’ve made that ambition very clear. It is open again and will be for some time, albeit with a smaller figure than the last time. That’s something that I’m working on at the moment.

“I think it’s not just about accessing the funding, for me, I think it’s also about showing that commitment to European solidarity, showing that commitment to working with our European colleagues and indeed others, [like] Canada is now in it as well, when it comes to our overall security,” she added. 

Niall O'Connor

news.title: Walls, windows and ceilings of Limerick house destroyed during ‘student party’
news.text:
Gardaí are investigating after a house in a Limerick city suburb was vandalised by youths attending a party.

The house, located at College Court, Castletroy, was designated a crime scene by gardaí, after walls and ceilings, and fixtures and fittings were torn down, in the early hours of Wednesday.

A video shared on social media showed young people throwing a shelving unit through a window of what appears to have been the property in question.

Other homes in the same estate and surrounding areas have been badly damaged in similar incidents over the years.

The video showed a group of suspected students screaming and laughing as more damage was caused to the property.

A male voice is heard shout “Oh my god,” as a wheelie bin is thrown at glass doors.

Walls and ceilings were also torn down in the property.

At one point during the video footage the camera is pointed up at a ceiling on the first floor, revealing no ceiling but a void into the attic and roofing joists.

The first floor of the property was also littered with what appeared to be attic and wall insulation, and fixtures and fittings in an upstairs bathroom were also destroyed.

“This is f*cked,” said another male on the video while a female voice is heard state “no lads, every f*cking room, welcome to our house tour”.

A local person at the scene said: “All the windows have been knocked out of it. A couple of students said there was a party there, they must have all gone berserk.”.

A garda spokeswoman said: “Gardaí received a report of an incident of criminal damage that occurred in College Court, Castletroy, Co Limerick, in the early hours of Wednesday morning 7th October 2026.”

The spokeswoman said gardaí conducted a “technical examination of the scene” and “investigations are ongoing”.

It was unclear if the youths filmed inside the property have any affiliation with University of Limerick (UL) which is located close to College Court.

However, in a statement, UL said it was “aware of an incident that took place off campus and that an investigation by An Garda Siochana is underway”.

“UL strongly promotes responsible behaviour and positive engagement with the community. While the vast majority of students are respectful and valued members of the community, the university recognises that instances of antisocial behaviour, including property damage, public disorder and other actions that negatively impact residents, are a matter of serious concern,” it said.

“There are mechanisms within the university student code of conduct for breaches of the code to be dealt with and complaints made to the University about individuals are taken very seriously.”
news.summary: Gardaí investigate damage caused to property in city in the early hours of Wednesday
news.author: David Raleigh

news.title: Covid-19 PPE fraudster jailed for scamming medical companies out of millions
news.text: A conman who defrauded medical firms of millions through bogus PPE transactions during the Covid-19 crisis has been imprisoned. Craig Morris, 43, along with his employer Jogesh Bhandari, 60, splashed out hundreds of thousands on high-end vehicles, timepieces, getaways and property after falsely claiming they could deliver millions of boxes of nitrile gloves to clients in the United States and Germany . Morris and Bhandari were found guilty of money laundering and conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation following a five-week trial at Leicester Crown Court in July. Bhandari's spouse, ex-pharmacist Meenakshi Bhandari, 58, was convicted of money laundering after the pair used the proceeds to purchase Rolexes and motors including an Audi A5, a Land Rover Discovery and a Porsche valued at £126,000. On Wednesday, Morris received a custodial sentence of three years and nine months at Northampton Crown Court, while Meenakshi Bhandari was given a two-year prison term, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity. The court was told that Jogesh Bhandari failed to appear at the hearing because he informed his legal representative he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" following a pacemaker procedure last week and was unable to make the journey to Northampton. Judge William Harbage KC proceeded to sentence the remaining two defendants in his absence as "the case cannot just be put off and put off at Mr Bhandari's will". The judge stated there is "no medical evidence" to adequately explain Jogesh Bhandari's absence from the sentencing hearing and a bench warrant will be issued for him. Prosecutor Michael Bisgrove told the court Jogesh Bhandari was the "driving force and the instigator" of the offending, while Morris was "very much working for" him. He said: "The offences took place during the Covid-19 pandemic at a time when there was a desperate shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE). "In that shortage, the offenders, particularly Mr Bhandari and Mr Morris, saw the opportunity to make money by fraud." The court was told that Jogesh Bhandari and Morris conducted fraudulent transactions through a company called Banton. He continued: "They pretended to be big players in the PPE market. They pretended to have PPE for sale and to be able to buy vast amounts of it." The court heard they swindled American company Med18 and German business MedTech by issuing contracts for equipment they didn't possess. Mr Bisgrove said: "In the course of the fraud, they took millions of pounds which they used for their own benefit – to buy cars, luxury goods and property." The court was informed the Bhandaris, from Mitchell Drive in Loughborough, Leicestershire, also utilised funds to settle family debts. Morris, from All Saints Road in Lytham St Annes, Lancashire, who has two teenage children, purchased a property, the court heard. The court was told that Jogesh Bhandari fraudulently obtained and retained £1.75 million, while Meenakshi Bhandari laundered funds totalling £960,000. The National Crime Agency (NCA) had previously revealed that Morris had been receiving regular payments of £5,000 from Jogesh Bhandari before the pair had a falling out at the end of 2021. Bhandari had been working alongside Frank Labruzzo, a US assistant attorney general at the Louisiana State Department of Justice, who facilitated a fraudulent escrow service – a bank account designed to hold funds until pre-agreed conditions are fulfilled. The court was also informed that Labruzzo and another individual involved in the scheme have since been convicted and sentenced in the United States . Jogesh Bhandari is due to be sentenced on October 16. When handing down sentences to Morris and Meenakshi Bhandari, Judge Harbage remarked that the pandemic was a period when "all of us had to make sacrifices and pull together for the good of society as a whole". He went on to say: "There were a few people though who sought to exploit that to make money for themselves, motivated by greed. "I'm satisfied Jogesh Bhandari and Craig Morris fall into that category."
news.summary: Craig Morris, 43, and his boss Jogesh Bhandari, 60, splashed hundreds of thousands of pounds on luxury cars, watches, holidays and a new home
news.author: Emma O'neill,Sophie Robinson Press Association

news.title: Watch: Heydon outlines initial details of fertiliser scheme
news.text:
Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine Martin Heydon has outlined some of the initial details of an upcoming fertiliser support scheme.

The scheme was announced as part of Budget 2027 yesterday (Tuesday, October 6).

Although the ins-and-outs of the scheme are yet to be finalised, Minister Heydon has outlined some details on how access to the scheme will operate, and what payments will be based on.

Speaking to Agriland, the minister said: "€77 million will go into farmers' pockets between now and the end of this year in cash injection, both with another run of the Fuel Income Support Scheme and with a newly-designed fertiliser scheme.

"€46.1 million I have for a fertiliser scheme. It will be based off last year's usage in 2025, off the [National] Fertiliser Database," the minister added.

He said: "I'm finalising details on that scheme, once I have the money this week. I had done significant work on it over the summer."

Minister Heydon indicated that farmer participation in the scheme will be based on the National Fertiliser Database, rather than on an application process.

He said: "I envisage that farmers won't have to apply for that, that I'll be able to do it in a way based off the database.

"I'll have to set minimum and maximum criteria and I'll engage with farm organisations on that before finalising the scheme," he added.

On the extended Fuel Income Support Scheme, Minister Heydon said it will be a "rerun of what people got earlier this year, again to be paid out before the end of this year".

Funding for both schemes will come from the underspend from the €100 million that was announced for the Fuel Income Support Scheme earlier this year.

"€38 million was spent of the €100 million I was allocated back in April... Of the €62 million remaining, €31 million will go on the Fuel Income Support Scheme again, paying the same amount out again before year-end," Minister Heydon said.

"Then on the fertiliser scheme, I received €15.4 million from the EU, as part of [Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen's] exceptional aid because of the impact of high prices on fertiliser," he explained.

"Member states were given the ability to add 200% to that figure that we each received, so that's another €31 million. So I have €62 million left out of the €100 million, €31 million is going on fuel, €31 million is going to the €15.4 million that we've got from the EU, so that's a €46 million fertiliser package," the minister added.

It is understood that memos will be brought to cabinet next week on these two schemes, which will be followed by talks with farm organisations on the fertiliser scheme to work through the final details.

Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine Martin Heydon has outlined some of the initial details of an upcoming fertiliser support scheme. 'Josh Ericson has been impressive... Todd Lawlor is very exciting'

Leinster hooker Dan Sheehan is happy to see young players making an impression.

6.31pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

DAN SHEEHAN IS raring to get his Leinster season going on the pitch, but he has enjoyed being part of the support crew for the past fortnight.

Sheehan was among the Ireland internationals who were part of Leinster’s URC tour of South Africa without playing in either game against the Lions and Sharks.

With those frontliners unavailable for match-day selection after their summer efforts with Ireland, a host of younger players made a positive impression for Leo Cullen’s side as they took three losing bonus points home.

Speaking on The 42 Rugby Weekly Extra podcast today, Sheehan picked out a couple of players who caught his eye in particular, namely 22-year-old number eight Josh Ericson and 20-year-old fullback Todd Lawlor.

“Josh has been very impressive,” said Sheehan.

“He kind of came out of nowhere into the pro circle a little bit last year; he played a lot of AIL for a while with Belvo, and I just thought he stepped up massively.

“You see him or you walk by him a few times and, you know, maybe he’s not the biggest fella, but he’s able to run over people. I thought the way he carried himself over the last two weeks and how physical he was in games was impressive.

“And then Todd Lawlor also making his debut down in South Africa, I thought he was very exciting to watch. A good person to have around the changing room, good craic but also a good running talent.

“We’ve seen it in training over the last few years. He probably had a bad season of injuries last year. But I remember him coming in, I think it was the start of last season when we all came back from the Lions tour, and he was training with us while the rest of the lads were off to South Africa, and you could see the talent in him.

Advertisement

“It’s nice to see him get his break like that and going well over the two weeks.”

Josh Ericson carrying the ball for Leinster.Steve Haag Sports / Christiaan Kotze/INPHO

Steve Haag Sports / Christiaan Kotze/INPHO / Christiaan Kotze/INPHO

Sheehan is fit and ready to go as Leinster get set for their competitive return to Laya Arena in Dublin when they face Cardiff this Saturday evening.

Having captained Ireland on their July tour of Australia and New Zealand in the Nations Championship, he enjoyed a five-week off-season before getting back into pre-season.

The return to training involved a fitness test, with a change-up from the ‘Bronco’ that has been done in recent years.

“It was ‘Double Efforts’ this year, which is a more forward-specific fitness test which involves a bit more down-up, backpedalling, shorter bursts,” said Sheehan. “But it’s also equally as grim as a Bronco.

“Josh van der Flier is always very good at it, as you can imagine, the perfect child.

“Do you know what? Tadhg Furlong is pretty good at that compared to the Bronco. He can bounce off the ground pretty well.”

With plenty of training under their belts now, Sheehan and his fellow Ireland frontliners are excited to get back into the swing of playing with Leinster.

The coming weeks include a big inter-pro against Munster at the Aviva Stadium, as well as the start of the Champions Cup away to Clermont before Ireland’s second Nations Championship window in November.

First up, it’s the homecoming game at Laya Arena.

“The changing room is buzzing to be back,” said Sheehan.

Laya Arena in Dublin.Eoin Burke / INPHO

Eoin Burke / INPHO / INPHO

“We were told that the redevelopment was going to happen, and then all of a sudden it’s two years, it was meant to be one-and-a-half years, and I think people are itching to get back in.

“We all have great memories of the RDS or the Laya Arena, whether it be debuts or big first European games or whatever it might be and going as a child.

“We owe it to the fans to make sure we show up properly and enjoy ourselves out there and put a performance in because it has probably been a different feel at Leinster games over the last two years, and we look forward to hopefully making this a proper home.

“I got to go to the Horse Show and obviously the Zebre pre-season game, and it’s a proper stadium, proper club ground, nice and intimate.

“The new stand is right on the pitch, you get access to players, and hopefully we can create a buzz for the season ahead because everyone in our changing room is excited to be back.”

Dan Sheehan was speaking ahead of Leinster Rugby’s homecoming game against Cardiff at Laya Arena on Saturday 10 October. Laya healthcare, part of AXA, is giving its members All Access to Leinster Rugby this season, with over 100 guests welcomed on the night and 5 lucky members invited to an upgraded hospitality experience. All Access will be at Leinster home games at Laya Arena all season, so follow @layahealthcare and @layaarena on Instagram for details.

Murray Kinsella

news.title: Gardaí investigate after student house damaged in Limerick
news.text:
Videos widely shared on social media show two young men throwing furniture through a window, shattering the glass, while others are heard laughing.

The footage shows extensive damage inside the house, including holes in walls and damage to part of the ceiling.

A Garda spokesperson told the Irish Examiner: "A technical examination of the scene has been conducted. Investigations are ongoing."

Some of the social media clips have since been taken down. 

One video was filmed by a young woman using Sabrina Carpenter's song House Tour, part of a social media trend in which users showcase their homes.

A University of Limerick spokesperson said it promotes responsible behaviour and takes incidents of anti-social conduct seriously.

While the vast majority of students make a positive contribution to the local community, the university acknowledged that issues such as property damage and public disorder are a source of serious concern.

The spokesperson said complaints involving students are investigated under the university's code of conduct.

"Students have been urged to be mindful of their actions and the impact they have on the community around them," the spokesperson said.
news.summary: A student property near the University of Limerick was extensively damaged in an incident that was filmed and shared on social media

'I've been called a lot worse': O'Donovan reacts to criticism and plays down reports of walkout

The Media Minister faced a litany of questions today about the various dramas involving him in the run up to the budget. 

6.21pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

DURING A LENGTHY post-budget press conference this afternoon, Media Minister Patrick O’Donovan played down reports that he stormed out of a budget meeting with Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers and brushed off criticism from an Irish language podcaster who said he is a “fucking eejit”.

In the lead-up to this year’s budget, O’Donovan found himself the subject of many news articles, with reports that he was locked in contentious arguments with both his junior minister Charlie McConalogue and the public expenditure minister. 

Last Friday, the Irish Examiner reported that O’Donovan walked out of a meeting with Chambers after just eight minutes because his budget requests were not being met.

O’Donovan made the €100 culture card for 16-year-olds a cornerstone of his budget asks this year, but the initiative, which would have cost between €7 and €8 million, was not greenlit by Chambers. 

Asked about the reports of a walkout today, O’Donovan said:

“When this press conference ends, regardless of however long or short it goes on I presume you will stand up from your seat and leave. I wouldn’t attribute that to being a walkout. 

“When a meeting ends, people naturally go about the rest of their lives.

“That’s what happens when a meeting ends.”

Separately, relations between O’Donovan and his junior minister for sport Charlie McConalogue have also reportedly soured in recent months.

The public row centred around which government party got to claim credit for new sports grants, with Fianna Fáilers unhappy Fine Gael TDs were beating them to the punch.

McConalogue and O'Donovan pictured today.Alamy

During an interview on Today with David McCullough on RTÉ Radio 1 last Friday, McConalogue failed to characterise relations with O’Donovan as “good” when asked. 

Asked today by a reporter if he was a liability to the government, given the number of arguments he has reportedly been involved in since he returned to work in September after a period of illness, O’Donovan said he did not “accept that assertion”.

Advertisement

“The most important group of people that have to like me are the people of County Limerick that gave us nearly 12,000 votes in the last election,” the minister said, adding:

“And after that, I have a job to do for the arts, culture, communications, media, and sports community in Ireland, given the seal of office that the president gave me to carry out my constitutional prerogatives.

“And if that means that I have to step on toes to stand up for the people who I am the minister with responsibility for, I’m sure that there’s other ministers that do that as well, and I’m not so sure that the word liability would attach to them.”

Asked how his relationship with Jack Chambers is, O’Donovan said it is “very good” and that they each have jobs to do and are both doing them.

On the timeline for the introduction of the culture card, O’Donovan said there are “things that we would have loved to have done this year, but we’ll get around to doing next year and the year after”.

“The concept of the culture card is not in any way going to be stopped,” he said. 

He added that he will be bringing a memorandum to government during 2027 on its development. 

It is worth noting, however, that Chambers said yesterday the card was “obviously” something that couldn’t be delivered next year.

Public sentiment

It was also put to O’Donovan that, given all the recent reports of arguments involving him, the public are “slightly exacerbated” by him. 

Specifically, it was put to him that during a recent episode of Irish language podcast How to Gael, during a discussion on comments O’Donovan made about Coimisiún na Meán, host Doireann Ní Ghlacáin said: 

“Can Patrick O’Donovan just take a day off from being a fucking eejit? Seriously?” 

Responding to this, the minister said he has been “called a lot worse than that”. 

“I’ve far more important things to answer than commentary like that. But I would like to say that the budget that I secured for the Department of Cultural, Communications and Sport will speak for itself,” he said, adding that it was “disappointing” that “very few” people raised his decision to continue funding for the basic income for the arts scheme.

Jane Matthews

news.title: 'Simply untenable': 1,200-bed DCU student development scrapped over soaring costs
news.text:
The development was to be delivered through a combination of State capital funding and university investment.

The Irish Examiner previously reported that planning permission was granted in 2019, with the first phase of the project, comprising 405 bed spaces, brought to tender in 2023.

However, Mr Raftery said inflation in construction costs meant accommodation charges would have had to rise to about €16,000 for an academic year in order to make the project viable.

He said DCU was unable to “bridge the viability gap” between construction costs and capital grant supports. It would require €6.7m more in State funding in order to develop the project and bring rents down to €9,500 for an academic year.

“The department took a view that they couldn’t go any further because of availability of funds or value for money at that point in time,” said Mr Raftery.

The project has now been put forward to the Higher Education Institution Student Accommodation Programme, with hopes to be developed in conjunction with private developers.

Private-public partnerships form the cornerstone of a national student accommodation strategy launched by higher education minister James Lawless earlier this year. Under the plan, private developers would build on university-owned land.

People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett questioned whether collaboration with private sector involvement was necessary in addressing the student bed deficit. The Department of Higher Education aims to unlock 42,000 more beds in the space of a decade as part of the plan.

Sinn Féin TD Donna McGettigan said students would rather see the strategy “ripped up and thrown in the bin".

Mr Raftery suggested that accommodation could be delivered more effectively by universities because they could avoid corporation tax and take loans at low interest levels, positing that straight builds from the private sector would run into similar issues and price out students.

Deirdre Lillis, president of Technological University Dublin, said that in an ideal world, student accommodation would be 100% publicly funded.

Experts before the committee cited a funding gap in the higher education sector, which is estimated to be an accumulated deficit of €780m over four years.

Higher education institutions have long struggled to meet demand for student accommodation, the committee heard.

University of Limerick chief operations officer for Campus Life Services, John O'Rourke, said 5,500 students were unsuccessful in securing on-campus accommodation this year. He warned that shortages disproportionately affect students from lower socio-economic backgrounds.

"Student accommodation is therefore no longer simply a housing issue, it's an issue of higher education, student success and access to higher education," he said.

The rent-a-room scheme has created approximately 250 student beds for UL students over the past four years.

Traffic gridlock in Cork

At the same committee meeting, MTU president Maggie Cusack said a lack of purpose-built student accommodation and transport infrastructure was creating an “appalling” gridlock centred around the college’s Bishopstown campus in Cork.

Ms Cusack said traffic was “creating a really poor student experience, quite appalling actually, thinking about the time our students are spending in cars".

“We’re literally driving all of the measures in the wrong direction, from climate to student experience."

Ms Cusack said housing was now the biggest barrier to student education.

"It saddens me to see large queues of traffic and to think that's the experience our students have day to day... We often think about what things cost, and I would challenge us to think of opportunity costs and what we're losing there."
news.summary: Lack of purpose-built student accommodation and transport infrastructure creating 'appalling' gridlock around MTU campus in Bishopstown
news.author: Alex Cunningham,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Social welfare Ireland: One major group is excluded from receiving the Christmas Bonus
news.text: In December, over a million people will receive a social welfare bonus ahead of Christmas. The bonus will be paid from the 7th of December, as confirmed in Budget 2027 earlier this week. Here's everything you need to know about it and who will receive the double week. A Christmas Bonus is paid to people getting long-term social welfare payments. You are paid a Christmas Bonus if you are getting: Back to Education Allowance - people coming from jobseeker's payments need to be getting the Allowance for at least 12 months (312 days), but you may be able to use your time on your jobseeker’s payment to help you qualify. Back to Work Enterprise Allowance - people coming from jobseeker's payments need to be getting the Allowance for at least 12 months (312 days), but you may be able to use time on jobseeker’s payment to help you qualify Back to Work Family Dividend Benefit Payment for 65 Year Olds Beneficiary of Temporary Protection Weekly Payment Bereaved Partner's Pension (Contributory) and (Non-Contributory) Blind Pension Carer's Allowance and Carer's Benefit (including half-rate Carer's Allowance) Community Employment Deserted Wife's Allowance and Deserted Wife's Benefit Daily Expenses Allowance for 12 months or more Disability Allowance Disablement Benefit Domiciliary Care Allowance Farm Assist Guardian's Payment (Contributory) and (Non-Contributory) Illness Benefit for 12 months or more Invalidity Pension Job Initiative Scheme Jobseeker's Allowance for 12 months (312 days or more) Jobseeker's Transitional payment Magdalene Commission Scheme Death Benefit Scheme (under the Occupational Injuries Scheme) One-Parent Family Payment Partial Capacity Benefit Rural Social Scheme State Pension (Contributory) and State Pension (Non-Contributory) Supplementary Welfare Allowance for 12 months (364 days or more) Tús Work Placement Experience Programme (if your primary payment is a qualifying social welfare payment) You will get a Christmas Bonus if you are getting a VTOS or Youthreach training allowance for at least 12 months subject to having an underlying DSP entitlement/qualifying payment (see list above). If you were getting a qualifying payment (see list above) immediately before your training allowance, you can combine this time to reach 12 months. If you live in a nursing home under the Fair Deal Scheme, your Christmas Bonus will not be counted as income or assessed under the Nursing Home Support Scheme. Fuel Allowance is not a qualifying payment for the Christmas Bonus. How much is the Christmas bonus? In 2025, the Christmas Bonus was 100% of your normal weekly payment. The minimum Bonus amount that is paid is €20. If an Increase for a Qualified Adult is paid directly to your dependent spouse, civil partner or cohabitant, the Christmas Bonus is also paid directly to them. If you are getting 2 eligible social welfare payments (for example, a One-Parent Family Payment and the Domiciliary Care Allowance or a half-rate Carer’s Allowance as well as your primary payment) you will get the Christmas Bonus for both payments. For Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA), which is paid monthly, the bonus is 100% of the weekly DCA rate. The DCA portion of the bonus is calculated independently of other payments. news.summary: The Christmas Bonus has been confirmed to return this December, with over a million people set to benefit from the double payment - here's the full list of those eligible and the key group that is excluded

news.title: Brian McFadden calls on teen singers as he searches for Ireland's next boy band
news.text: Brian McFadden is on the search for Ireland's next big boy band and is calling on aspiring singers aged between 17 and 19. The singers are being invited to put their voices, personalities and passion for music to the test in the hope of becoming part of a new Irish pop group. Leading the search is former Westlife star Brian McFadden , who brings first-hand experience of life in one of Ireland’s most successful boybands. McFadden rose to fame as a member of Westlife in the late 1990s, with the group achieving a string of chart-topping hits. He went on to pursue a successful solo career, with his debut single ‘Real to Me’ reaching number one, and continues to tour today as part of BoyzLife. Joining McFadden on the search will be Sarah Gallagher, founder of NDA Talent, who has more than 20 years’ experience in music management. Gallagher spent 17 years with Modest Management, the company behind the careers of major acts including One Direction, JLS and Little Mix, while personally managing Olly Murs and working on the comeback of Five. She now manages the careers of Olly Murs and Five through NDA Talent. Also joining the panel is Paul Franklin, a highly regarded senior music agent based in London, currently representing talent at Creative Artists Agency (CAA), one of the world’s leading entertainment agencies. With extensive experience across international touring, artist development and the pop and boyband world, Franklin has worked with major artists including Amy Winehouse, Mariah Carey, Demi Lovato, James Bay, Jessie J, McFly, Busted, Five, The Saturdays, The Vamps and The Wanted. Speaking about the search, Brian McFadden said, “I’m really excited to be putting together a brand-new Irish boyband and discovering the next generation of talent. We’re looking for lads aged 17 to 19 who have great voices, personality, ambition and, most importantly, a passion for music. Ireland has always produced incredible talent, and I believe the next big boyband is out there waiting to be discovered. This could be a life-changing opportunity, so if you think you’ve got what it takes, we want to hear from you!” Aspiring singers aged 17 to 19 who believe they have what it takes to become part of the new group are being encouraged to apply online via https://eu.castitreach.com/a/mmm/irishboyband/audition . Applications will close on Sunday, 25th of October at 5pm. Applicants will be contacted with details of an in-person audition in Dublin, with further information to be provided in due course. Center Parcs Longford Forest is a large resort that takes up 400 acres of forest a short drive from Ballymahon.

'Small number' of workers at Center Parcs at risk of redundancy

It is unclear the exact number and types of roles at risk.

5.57pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

LAST UPDATE

CENTER PARCS HAS confirmed that a “small number” of roles at its holiday resort in Co Longford “may be at risk of redundancy”.

The Department of Enterprise confirmed this evening to The Journal that it was notified of proposed collective redundancies by the company on Monday.

A company of its size that intends to make 30 or more people redundant within a 30-day period is required to notify the Department.

Center Parcs Longford Forest is a large resort that takes up 400 acres of forest a short drive from Ballymahon. It is a hugely successful holiday destination for both those in Ireland and abroad, and is popular with families.

Last year, its accounts showed it was raking in close to €2 million a week in revenue.

Advertisement

However, the company said it has begun “a review of some of our structures to make sure they remain right for our business today and for the future”.

A spokesperson for Center Parcs Ireland told The Journal: “Sadly, this means a small number of roles may be at risk of redundancy.

“We recognise the significant impact this uncertainty can have on colleagues and their families, and we are committed to supporting everyone affected with care and respect throughout the consultation process.”

The resort employs a large amount of people locally, reporting 1,268 staff members in 2025.

It is unclear the number and types of roles at risk.

The resort this year saw €100 million invested into the site, resulting in an additional 83 lodges, which pushed its occupancy capacity to around 3,500. Facilities were also upgraded and new amenities made available.

Emma Hickey

news.title: Martin King and Jenny McCarthy's key to a happy marriage ahead of anniversary milestone
news.text: Martin King and Jenny McCarthy have shared their secret to a long and happy marriage as they prepare for an anniversary milestone. The Ireland AM presenter and photographer got married in a beautiful winter wedding in November 2011 and are set to mark 15 years since the big day next month. They tied the knot in the stunning Killashee Hotel in Naas and it's such a special day for them. The couple told RSVP Magazine: "It was a fairly traditional wedding with all the people who mattered most to us there. Looking back now, we think what made it so lovely was that it was really about celebrating us and having our family and friends together. "There were nerves, of course, but mostly we remember feeling really happy and excited that this was actually happening. There’s something very surreal about getting ready in the morning knowing that by the end of the day you’re going to be married to the person you love." See inside Martin and Jenny's wedding through the gallery below... The special day was full of sweet moments. "Honestly, it’s the little moments that stand out," Martin and Jenny gushed. "Seeing each other for the first time, being surrounded by our five children, family and friends and just the sheer happiness of the day. As if it was written in the stars, Dublin won their first All-Ireland in 16 years with a last-minute free by Stephen Cluxton and Jenny organised for Sam Maguire to arrive at the wedding as a surprise for GAA mad Martin. That moment was epic for all of Martin’s family, especially his dad." They added: "We also remember the laughter and the craic, because that’s very much us! And now, 15 years on, we think one of the loveliest things is looking back at photographs and remembering people and moments that you might otherwise have forgotten." Now as they prepare to celebrate their anniversary soon, the couple shared their secret to a happy relationship: "Friendship, laughter and not taking each other for granted and also making time for each other, even if it’s just sitting together to watch TV. Being able to laugh together, we think that’s hugely important. After 15 years, you realise marriage isn’t about everything being perfect. It’s about choosing each other, again and again, through all the different stages of life." This interview originally appeared in the September issue of RSVP Magazine. The Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund was allocated €102 million in Budget 2027.Alamy Stock Photo

Greyhound Racing

State funding for greyhound racing exceeds €20m for the first time in 25 years

The sector’s funding has gone up by half a million compared with 2026.

6.11pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

THE GREYHOUND RACING industry has received over €20 million in funding for the first time since the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund was established in 2001. 

The fund, which is overseen by the Department of Agriculture, was allocated €102 million in Budget 2027 – an increase of €2.9 million from last year.

The money is split 80:20 between the two sports, with horse racing to receive €79.3 million of the fund and greyhound racing to receive €20.4 million. 

Announcing the allocation, Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon said: “The proposed increase in the Fund will be linked to the implementation of the Indecon Review’s recommendations in respect of equine and greyhound welfare and integrity. This will form part of the Department’s overall animal welfare package.”

The government has come under fire for consistently funding the industry despite ethical concerns around the sport. The funding is in the context of analysis which shows dwindling popularity among the public.

Greyhound Racing Ireland has welcomed the allocation and said the industry is “well-regulated” and “ethical”, and that it makes a significant contribution to Ireland’s economy and culture.

A 2021 report on greyhound racing estimated the industry contributed €132.3 million annually to the Irish economy; however, Sinn Féin senator Chris Andrews previously said the figure could be as low as around €49 million.

Speaking to The Journal, Andrews said funding for the industry is down to intense lobbying of Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil and “undue influence over public policy”.

“Since 2001, successive Governments have handed €407 million of public money to the inhumane and unpopular greyhound industry. Next year, greyhound racing will receive over €20 million from the state, up half a million from 2026,” he said.

Andrews compared the funding to that of the League of Ireland, which received just €4 million in funding in Budget 2027, despite a report finding it contributed over €160 million to the economy in 2023. 

Andrews said: “This funding is far and away more than what is being given to the League of Ireland, which has to fight for scraps while Greyhound Racing Ireland is guaranteed a mountain of cash every year in perpetuity.”

“Over 1.1 million people attended League of Ireland matches last year. Greyhound meets attracted only a third of that number, and yet the Government barely has an interest in investing in Irish football.”

😡😡😡😡€102 million 😡😡😡❤️❤️
That’s an extraordinary amount of public money being spent on horse and greyhound racing, while animal rescues across Ireland are struggling to survive.💔💔
Those same rescues are taking in the horses and greyhounds who have been discarded, neglected and traumatised. They are paying for veterinary care, rehabilitation, food, shelter and the chance of a second life, often relying on donations and volunteers just to keep going.💔

And yet, our Government continues to put enormous public funding into an industry built around racing and betting.😡😡😡

How can this be right?

While rescues are fighting every single day to repair the damage done to these animals, where is the same commitment to their welfare?

This isn’t just about money. It’s about priorities. It’s about what kind of country we want Ireland to be.

Animals cannot speak for themselves. We have to speak for them.💔💔😡😡😡😡

😡Contact the Taoiseach:😡
Email: taoiseach@taoiseach.gov.ie
Phone: 01 619 4000
Address: Department of the Taoiseach, Government Buildings, Merrion Street Upper, Dublin 2, D02 R583— My Lovely Horse Rescue (@MyLovelyHorseR) October 6, 2026

Advertisement

Meanwhile, People Before Profit’s Paul Murphy described the funding as “outrageous”.

Speaking to The Journal, he said: “Why is the public paying for cruel greyhound racing? Why is the public giving money for horse racing prizes which end up as tax-free money in the pockets of some of the richest people in the country?”

Sinn Féin’s Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh believes horse racing and greyhound racing should be decoupled when it comes to funding. 

“Greyhound racing should be required to demonstrate its viability as a standalone industry before receiving further taxpayer support,” she told The Journal.

“At present, the industry benefits from being tied to the far more lucrative horse racing sector, despite declining attendance and growing public concern about animal welfare.”

Greyhound advocacy group Greyhound Action said the funding of industry in the budget is “unjustifiable from either an economic or animal welfare perspective”.

“The greyhound racing industry is losing money; it has chronically poor attendance at its stadia and its economic case for state support relies on outdated evidence,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

“Most damningly of all, it’s an industry whose animal welfare record raises profound questions about whether it should even be allowed to continue.”

The group called on the government to commission an independent, transparent and up-to-date study of the economic value of greyhound racing to the economy.

Animal rescue charity My Lovely Horse criticised the government for funding the industry while animal rescues struggle financially.

“Those same rescues are taking in the horses and greyhounds who have been discarded, neglected and traumatised,” it said on X.

“They are paying for veterinary care, rehabilitation, food, shelter and the chance of a second life, often relying on donations and volunteers just to keep going.”

Greyhound Racing Ireland, also known as Rásaíocht Con Éireann, said it welcomed the government’s announcement and is “looking forward to continuing to govern and deliver a well-regulated, ethical sport and industry; which through its regularly published performance data demonstrates that it has the greyhound’s welfare as its key strategic priority, and is at the forefront of animal welfare governance in the country”.

“RCÉ as a Commercial Semi-State Body, and the wider greyhound racing industry, also make a significant contribution to the economy and the social, cultural and heritage life of our country.”

Horse Racing Ireland and the Department of Agriculture have been contacted for comment. 

Sophie Finn
