Budget 2027

Tánaiste says he wants to build on inheritance tax changes in future budgets 

A number of TDs were disappointed there were no reforms for those without children. 

5.12pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

THE INHERITANCE TAX changes in this year’s budget are “a step” in the right direction with Tánaiste and finance minister Simon Harris telling The Journal that the government plans to build on it in future budgets. 

Since new budget measures were voted in on Tuesday night, the threshold at which capital acquisitions tax kicks in has increased.

A child can now inherit €420,000 from their parents in their lifetime before capital acquisitions tax of 33% kicks in – up from €400,000 previously. 

The threshold for siblings, nieces, nephews and some other relatives has also increased from €40,000 to €44,000.

For non-relatives, the threshold has increased from €20,000 to €22,000.

Asked about the changes after the budget announcement on Tuesday, Harris said the government could not go further as the fiscal space available in the budget would not allow it this year.

Additional movement on the thresholds “would have cost a lot more than we had available,” said Harris.

Once it was decided by the government that the budget must include a personal tax package, there was limited scope for other measures, with Harris stating that he was pleased he managed to get increases in all three inheritance categories.

Advertisement

Speaking about the changes made, Harris added: 

It is a step and I hope it is something we can build on in the years ahead.

Inheritance tax has seen significant changes in Ireland following the 2008 financial crisis.

In 2008, people in Group A could inherit over €521,000 tax-free, before a tax of 20% was charged.

Between 2008 and 2012, tax-free thresholds on inheritances were steadily decreased while the rate of CAT was increased. 

Harris acknowledged that the changes made on budget day will not satisfy those who want equalisation of the inheritance tax system, particularly those who do not have children and want reforms so they can leave assets to a chosen beneficiary. 

TDs advocate for people who do not have children

During the vote on Tuesday evening on the inheritance tax changes, a number of TDs criticised the government for not taking the opportunity for wider reforms to the system. 

Independent Ireland TD Michael Collins said there were a lot of promises and soundings made that have not been delivered on.

“The bottom line is that this needs to be looked at again. I am pleading with the minister to look at it again and to give everybody a chance,” he said. 

Kerry TD Michael Healy-Rae said he warmly welcomed the changes.

However, he added:

Related Reads

Budget 2027: What changed at midnight - and what we'll have to wait for

Budget 2027 includes income tax band change, carbon tax freeze, and price hike on cigarettes

Rate of deemed disposal tax on investment funds to reduce to 35% from January 

“People who get married, or not, and who do not produce children of their own and do not have what we call direct heirs, those people work very hard. It might be their own house or a second house, or it might be a farm of land and when they eventually pass on, they see their asset being devalued so much because whoever they give it to will have to pay so much inheritance tax on it.

“I know that everything cannot be done all together at the same time but I would be very much hoping that in the future, we will be able to look at those categories of people and do something more to help them.”

However, Sinn Féin’s David Cullinane said he was not in favour of the inheritance tax changes, stating that “Fine Gael represents a cosseted, privileged class”.

“I do not know of many people who are looking for changes to inheritance tax… 

“The scandalous part about this resolution is that if a house is sold for €800,000 and two children benefit from it, they will not pay a single cent in inheritance tax,” he said.

People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy said only a small number of people are impacted by inheritance tax.

“Most people do not get that. Only a third of people get any substantial inheritance whatsoever in the course of their entire lifetime. The average inheritance that people get is about €100,000,” he said.

“It is the most well-off, most comfortable people who will benefit from this tax change at a time when the majority of people are struggling with the cost of living crisis,” added Murphy.

news.title: Teen who abused very young half-sisters caught when mother walked in - and he was recording on phone
news.text: A teenager jailed for two years for the “appalling” abuse of his two very young half-sisters will also be subject to an eight-year post release supervision order, a court has ruled. The Central Criminal Court heard that the abuse came to light in March 2023 after the children’s mother walked into the boy’s room and saw him abusing his five-year-old half-sister while recording it on his phone. His then two-year-old half-sister was also in the room. The now 18-year-old pleaded guilty to multiple counts including three of sexually assaulting the older half-sister and one of orally raping her, and two of sexually assaulting the younger half-sister. He further pleaded guilty to charges of sexually exploiting his half-sisters, of engaging in sexual activity in the presence of a child and the production, possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), known in law as child pornography. The investigation found a video of the boy masturbating on a bus, the court heard. In September 2023, after the abuse of his half-sisters was discovered, he was found viewing CSAM on a school laptop during a class. The court was told this was material obtained from the internet. In total, seven videos were identified, including six assessed as in the most serious category. The boy was today handed a four-year sentence with the final two years suspended on very strict conditions for four years. He will also be subject to the Sex Offender’s Act for five years and an eight-year post release supervision order. The boy was between 14 and 15 when he abused his half-sisters in the family home, on various dates between 2022 and 2023. He cannot be named as all parties have a legal right to anonymity Their mother sent files to her phone after discovering the abuse before deleting them from the boy’s phone. Gardai are satisfied the woman’s sole concern was to preserve any evidence for future investigations, the court was told. When the boy’s phone was analysed, 408 images and 11 videos of CSAM were found, including some of him sexually abusing both girls. One video also showed the boy masturbating on a school bus. Thousands of videos and images of adult pornography were also found. The boy was sent the next day to stay with his father, but returned to sit his Junior Certificate. He then went back to his father’s home for the summer before going back to school. While there was a safety plan, it later became clear that the boy couldn’t remain in the family home. He went into specialised foster care, as he could not live with others under 18. More recently, he has been living in an aftercare placement and completed his Leaving Certificate online. The court was told that the boy also distributed images of the abuse of the older girl on a particular social media app. He also shared material of himself with a Snapchat user. Gardai consider this to be a ‘catfish’ account, pretending to be the boy’s peer. The boy told gardai he stored images in case this Snapchat user got back in touch. The court heard there was no evidence of blackmail or threats and the boy was himself exploited. However, it was noted he continued the abuse after contact from this account had stopped. After hearing the facts earlier this year, Mr Justice Paul McDermott agreed to a defence application to allow the boy complete his Leaving Certificate and a therapeutic programme. However, there had been concerns in recent months that the boy was not fully complying with his strict bail conditions. The court heard earlier this week that the boy was seen by a case worker with a mobile phone in August. Michael Bowman SC, defending, said his client is aware he can’t have a phone. “It’s an easy thing for everyone to say but for an 18-year-old boy in that world, it’s an exceeding difficult place to find himself. It doesn’t excuse it but that is the reality”. Mr Justice McDermott remanded the boy into custody earlier this week and finalised sentence. The judge noted this case was about “very disturbing behaviour” by a young teenager who had repeatedly abused his “very young” sisters over a protracted period. He said the court had viewed the recording made on the day the abuse was discovered, describing the footage as “appalling” and noting its serious nature. The judge said the mother had been placed in the “most difficult position imaginable” and had “done her very best by each of her three children”. He said the recording of the abuse was aggravating and that the boy had breached parental and sibling trust. Reports from a forensic psychologist, the Probation Service and the National Interagency Prevention Programme (NIAPP) were reviewed by the court. The boy is assessed at high risk of re-offending with the Probation Service stating his risk factors include a preoccupation with this kind of abuse, an attraction to children, difficulties repressing urges, and viewing pornography, which the court considered a factor in his offending. A multidisciplinary structure is considered necessary by adult services due to the level of risk the boy presents. The judge noted that the boy’s bail conditions included that he hand over his laptop for school online to care workers at night, with the aim of limiting his online access. Last month, the boy admitted to buying and selling ten smart phones since his 18 th birthday, downloading certain apps, viewing pornography and having a “deviant sexual interest in young girls”. The judge noted one recent report states the boy views his use of pornography as appropriate. Services concluded that his engagement wasn’t meaningful and fully honest. Mr Justice McDermott said that the boy had deceived gardai and support services and that an “enormous effort” had been made to assist his rehabilitation. It had been believed this a community-based approach was working, but this has been undermined by the boy’s failure to fully comply with his bail conditions. The boy also led others to believe he was dealing with issues honestly when he wasn’t, the judge said. Mr Justice McDermott indicated that a “different approach is now required” and that a custodial sentence would be imposed. The judge noted both girls have received counselling and the family decided not to make a victim impact statement. He said the court respected this decision, and considered that “terrible damage” had been done to the girls and to the family unit. The judge outlined the headline sentences which would apply on each count for an adult, including 12 years for the oral rape. He reduced each headline sentence to reflect that the boy was a child in the eyes of the law at the time of the offending, reducing the headline sentence for oral rape to six years. The judge also noted the mitigation including the boy’s early guilty pleas, admissions, his social isolation and exploitation by others. Mr Justice McDermott suspended the final two years of the global four-year sentence to incentivise his engagement with services and to supervise his return to the community. The conditions for the part-suspended sentence include that the boy engage with any programmes to address his sexual offending. He must also have no contact with the victims, stay away from playgrounds and school grounds and have no contact or be in the company of any child under 18 unless another adult is present. The judge directed these conditions apply to the eight-year post release supervision order. The court previously heard that the family home was searched in May 2023, and a letter written by the boy to his parents, which contained some admissions, was handed over. In the letter, he acknowledged sexually abusing his younger sisters and said his behaviour changed due to watching pornography. No disclosure was initially made by the five-year-old girl, but she later spoke to social workers. She disclosed abuse by her older brother to specialist gardai in October 2023. She said she was scared of the boy and that he made her watch scary things. She said he touched her inappropriately on several occasions. Maurice Coffey SC, prosecuting, noted that gardai obtained limited evidence from talking to the girl, given her limited vocabulary and age-appropriate understanding of the situation. The two-year-old girl was not interviewed by gardai. A full Tusla investigation also took place. The boy made admissions when he was separately interviewed by Tulsa and gardai. He admitted ownership of 60 Google accounts, three X (formerly Twitter) accounts and other social media accounts. The court heard his mother is willing to allow him to remain in her life, so long as he addresses his offending behaviour. news.title: Two Cork men appear in court following €500k cannabis seizure
news.text:
Cannabis weighing 25 kilos with a street value of €500,000 was seized in Togher and two men were arrested and brought before Cork District Court today

Lee Crinnion (21) from Blackwater Grove, Togher, Cork, and 25-year-old Aaron Austin of Araglen Court, Togher, Cork, were arrested by Detective Garda Darren Twomey and Det Garda Ruairi McGovern, respectively, from the Cork City Divisional Drugs Unit.

Both of them were charged with possession of cannabis and having the cannabis for sale or supply at Togher Road, Cork on Monday, October 5.

Neither of them made any reply to the charges when they were put to them after caution.

Judge David Waters asked Det Garda Twomey if the value of drugs in the case was significant and if it was likely to stay in the district court. The detective said that the value was substantial at €500,000 and would eventually be dealt with at a higher court.

Sergeant David Fleming said that gardaí were not objecting to bail with conditions. 

Defence solicitors Joseph Cuddigan and Eddie Burke confirmed that their clients were consenting to the bail terms after discussing them with the investigating gardaí.

Conditions included an 11pm to 7am curfew, signing on three times a week at Togher Garda Station, surrendering their passports and not apply for any other travel documents, providing gardaí with mobile phone numbers on which they could be contacted at all times, and that they would have no contact with each other directly or indirectly.

Judge Waters remanded both men on bail to appear again at Cork District Court on November 3 for the DPP’s directions.
news.summary: Lee Crinnion and Aaron Austen were charged with possession of cannabis and having the cannabis for sale or supply at Togher Road, Cork on Monday, October 5

news.title: Cork bathing locations see 'excellent' results after summer monitoring
news.text:
Cork’s bathing waters have enjoyed an exceptionally strong season, with all monitored waters returning “excellent” results to date and 10 beaches holding Blue Flag status. The county also has 12 Green Coast awards, according to Cork County Council’s latest bathing water report.

Brendan Meagher, the council’s acting county engineer, said the sunny weather had helped conditions during the season. The data covers 30 beaches across the county, including 13 designated bathing waters monitored under the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) programme.

One beach holds both a Blue Flag and a Green Coast award, while nine hold Blue Flags only and 12 have Green Coast awards. The council said all designated bathing waters had achieved excellent results so far this year.

Two new locations were added to the monitoring programme for 2026: White Bay in Cork Harbour and the Blue Pool in Glengarriff. Monitoring on Cape Clear has also moved to North Harbour, which the council said offers a safer and more accessible bathing location.

Social Democrats’ Isobel Towse welcomed the move, saying it made sense to monitor the more sheltered North Harbour as it is the part of Cape Clear most frequented by swimmers. She said it was important that water quality there continued to be monitored.

There was one significant incident during the season, when Cadogan’s Strand in Schull was closed as a precaution after reports of discoloured water. Investigations found no evidence of contamination and the bathing area reopened within three days.

The council is continuing investigative work at The Warren, or Cregane Strand, in Rosscarbery and at Fountainstown. DNA source tracking is being used to identify the origin of any contamination and support corrective action.

Strong results this season could support the return of Blue Flag status for Fountainstown and Garryvoe, although the council said this depended on continued performance for the remainder of the season.

It is also too early to determine whether Fountainstown or The Warren will regain their flags for 2027.

Funded by the Local Democracy Reporting Scheme.
news.summary: The data covers 30 beaches across the county, including 13 designated bathing waters monitored under the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) programme.
news.author: David Forsythe,EchoLive.ie

news.title: Eirgrid hosts event on windfarm locations in Aghada until 8pm tonight
news.text:
EirGrid is continuing its public information events across Cork to discuss the development of onshore and offshore electricity grid infrastructure for the south coast of Ireland.

The events will provide an opportunity for the public, communities and stakeholders to share their feedback on proposed onshore and offshore station locations, landfall sites and grid connection points.

A public consultation open day, from 12 noon – 8pm, is taking place today at Aghada Community Centre and there will be another open day in Garryvoe Hotel on Wednesday November 4.

There will also be mobile unit information stands available on October 27 at Garryvoe beach carpark from 10am – 1pm and in Cloyne GAA carpark from 2pm – 5pm.

The public information events are part of EirGrid's Powering Up Offshore – South Coast programme, which aims to build the transmission grid infrastructure required to connect offshore wind generation to the national grid.

Sinéad Dooley, head of public engagement at EirGrid, said she is encouraging people to attend our consultation events in Cork where they can meet the project team, learn more about the proposals and have their say.

“Local knowledge and stakeholder feedback are critical to helping shape the next stage of the project, and we want as many people as possible to get involved in the consultation process."

“This consultation is an important milestone in the development of the programme. The emerging best performing options we are presenting have been informed by extensive technical and environmental studies, as well as engagement with stakeholders, and we now want to hear directly from communities and interested parties on these proposals.”
news.summary: The next public consultation open day, from 12 noon – 8pm, takes place tonight at Aghada Community Centre and there will be another open day in Garryvoe Hotel on Wednesday November 4.

news.title: Cork man accused of recording 'partially undressed' women in Dublin Airport toilets
news.text:
A book of evidence has been served today on a 31-year-old Cork man accused of recording partially undressed females in a toilet area of Dublin Airport last year.

Garda Denis Callanan charged Eric O’Neill of Delford Drive, Rochestown Road, with a single count in relation to the alleged offence and this week in court he was served with a book of evidence.

On the application of Sergeant Gearóid Davis at Cork District Court, Judge David Waters sent the case forward to the next sessions of Cork Circuit Criminal Court commencing on October 27. The defendant was represented by solicitor Shane Collins-Daly.

The charge against him states that on April 19 2025 at Dublin Airport, he did engage in offensive conduct of a sexual nature, namely the recording of females in a partially undressed state within the confines of the ladies bathroom/toilets within Dublin Airport, contrary to the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017.
news.summary: Garda Denis Callanan charged Eric O’Neill of Delford Drive, Rochestown Road, with a single count in relation to the alleged offence.

news.title: New papal nuncio likely to continue radical downsizing of Catholic dioceses in Ireland
news.text:
A new papal nuncio to Ireland has been appointed by the Vatican from Poland. Archbishop Jan Romeo Pawlowski (65) is currently papal nuncio in Greece. 

He was born in 1960 in Biskupiec, northern Poland, and was ordained in 1985 before studying for a doctorate in canon law at the Gregorian University in Rome.

Pawlowski then entered the Vatican’s diplomatic service and was made archbishop in 2009 when appointed papal nuncio to the Republic of the Congo and Gabon. 

In 2015 he returned to the Vatican, serving as its secretariat of state becoming head of its section for diplomatic staff in 2017. In 2022 he was appointed papal nuncio to Greece.

He speaks Italian, French, Russian, English, German and Portuguese.

A papal nuncio is effectively the Vatican’s ambassador to Ireland. He will also automatically become dean of the diplomatic corps in the State.

In church terms his primary role is in the appointment of bishops, making recommendations to Rome. More recently in Ireland the nuncio has also played a key role in the reduction of Irish Catholic dioceses.

[ Called to the church: ‘I broke her heart but I felt I could do more for people by being a priest’Opens in new window ]

The new nuncio succeeds Archbishop Luis Mariano Montemayor (70), who served in Ireland from February 2023 until July this year, when he retired. 

In his three years, Archbishop Montemayor, originally from Argentina and another Vatican career diplomat, oversaw some of the most radical changes in the structure of the Irish Catholic Church in 900 years, with a significant reduction in the number of dioceses.

In 1111, at the Synod of Ráth Breasail, Ireland’s current diocesan structure was set up.

Some “downsizing” had taken place before Archbishop Montemayor’s arrival in 2023. In 2021 Clonfert was joined with Galway. But on his watch this process was sped up, with Achonry joining Elphin in 2025 and, earlier this year, Killala with Tuam. It meant six west of Ireland Catholic dioceses were reduced to three. 

Last July, Ossory diocese – mainly Kilkenny – was similarly joined under one bishop, with Ferns diocese, mainly Wexford.

[ ‘My proposal was to stop Confirmation’: Ireland’s ageing priests under pressure as numbers dropOpens in new window ]

When it came to the appointment and transfer of bishops, Archbishop Montemayor was similarly active. He appointed Fr Paul Connell Bishop of Ardagh and Clonmacnoise in 2023 and Fr Donal Roche as auxiliary bishop of Dublin in 2024. 

In 2024 he oversaw the transfer of then Bishop of Raphoe (Donegal) Alan McGuckian SJ to Down and Connor diocese, mainly Belfast and Antrim. Also that year, then bishop of Achonry Paul Dempsey became an auxiliary bishop of Dublin. 

In 2025 Bishop of Elphin Kevin Doran was named also Bishop of Achonry, while last February, Archbishop of Tuam Francis Duffy was named Bishop of Killala.

Last year too Bishop of Ossory Niall Coll was transferred to Raphoe diocese. Last February, Archbishop of Tuam Francis Duffy was also named Bishop of Killala while last July Auxiliary Bishop of Armagh Michael Router, was appointed Bishop of Derry and Bishop of Ferns Ger Nash was also named Bishop of Ossory. 

It is likely such downsizing will continue under Archbishop Pawlowski.

More immediately, both Bishop of Clogher (mainly Monaghan) Larry Duffy and Bishop of Cloyne (mainly east Cork) William Crean are due to retire later this year, and there has been speculation for some time that Clogher may be joined with its neighbour Kilmore (mainly Cavan) and Cloyne with Cork and Ross diocese.

Further, since 2018 the Catholic Primate and Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin has been administrator of the small Co Down diocese of Dromore. It followed the resignation of then Bishop of Dromore John McAreavey in a controversy over his handling of child abuse allegations against the late Fr Malachy Finnegan. That arrangement is expected to be formalised.
news.summary: Polish nuncio succeeds Archbishop Montemayor, who oversaw some of most radical changes in 900 years
news.author: Patsy McGarry

pace of reform

The government has cut RTÉ's funding by €20m - and Kevin Bakhurst is not happy about it

The director-general said the decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.

4.56pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

RTÉ DIRECTOR GENERAL Kevin Bakhurst has said he “completely rejects the assertion” that the pace of reform within the national broadcaster has been slow, after it was confirmed in Budget 2027 that it would receive €20 million less in funding. 

In 2024, the government committed to providing public funding of €725 million to RTÉ from licence fee receipts and a direct top-up from the Exchequer over three years.

Of this, €260 million was allocated for 2027.

However, media minister Patrick O’Donovan today confirmed that the funding for next year would amount to €240 million. This is made up of €66 million in direct exchequer support, and €174 million in projected licence fee collections. 

Speaking at a post-budget briefing, he said the figure “is less than envisaged by the government in 2024" but reflects “the overall funding available to my department”.

“It is also in the context of progress made by RTÉ in the delivery of their strategy,” O’Donovan said.

“While progress has been made across a number of issues, I am not happy that we have seen sufficient progress in delivering the smaller, more agile organisation that wants to be delivered under the strategy.”

He also said RTÉ will receive an €11 million “uplift” instead of a planned €31 million, adding that “we were simply not in that space to be able to do that”.

Bakhurst says ‘extensive reform delivered’

In a statement this afternoon, Bakhurst said the government’s decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.

“RTÉ welcomed and was grateful for the Government’s commitment in 2024 to provide public funding to RTÉ of €725 million over three years, from 2025 – 2027,” he said.

“In fact, the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste said at the time, that predictable multi-annual funding is key to RTÉ being able to deliver a strategy.”

Bakhurst said the decision to cut funding was coming at a “late stage”, when the organisation has “already made important commitments to our audiences, to the independent sector, to other important stakeholders and to RTÉ staff”. 

He said the three-year funding commitment allowed RTÉ to plan ahead and, among other things, deliver independent news and analysis, commit to producing more public service programmes, invest in podcasts and the RTÉ Player, and stabilise its finances. 

“We completely reject the assertion that the pace of reform and transformation within RTÉ has been slow,” he said.

Advertisement

“The Leadership Team and I have delivered extensive reform since I took up the role of Director-General, including implementation of around 90% of the EAC report recommendations.

“We have also already managed to exit almost 100 people from the organisation, despite the late approval of the Voluntary Exit Programme and a short window to enable people to leave.”

Bakhurst said RTÉ board chair Terence O’Rourke was seeking a meeting with O’Donovan about the matter, “particularly given that RTÉ has committed to numerous agreements with its stakeholders based on this written and extensively publicised agreement.

He concluded by saying: “If the three-year multi-annual agreement will no longer be honoured – we now have some important decisions to make.”

‘Not an insignificant amount of money’

When asked about Bakhurst’s statement at the briefing, O’Donovan said public service organisations across a number of sectors have had to demonstrate key efficiencies being delivered over the last 12 months.

Media minister Patrick O'Donovan speaking at a post-budget briefing this afternoon.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

The Fine Gael minister said his department was “a very agency-dependent department” and had “very little scope, to be quite honest, about it in relation to where the resources that we had available to us needed to be assigned”.

He said it was “well-documented” that there were “issues” regarding RTÉ’s voluntary redundancy, something he said “he hopes “would be able to be advanced and ameliorated”.

An internal analysis of the redundancy programme found that substantial work had been put into preparing early exit packages for staff, but only a relatively small number eventually received offers.

O’Donovan said his department would continue to engage with RTÉ on a weekly basis, and noted that €240 million “is not an insignificant amount of money”.

“It’s a quarter of a billion, and there are very few organisations across the state that can point to resource allocation of that order, and it certainly represents an enormous part of the current expenditure amount that is available to me as minister to be able to allocate.”

He concluded by saying he would update the government shortly on the delivery of the RTÉ reform program, “including on progress made and what is yet to be achieved”. 

At the Public Accounts Committee in July, Bakhurst told TDs and senators that RTÉ was “tightening its belt” as it strengthened its financial position and “reversed the trend of reporting deficits” as a result of tighter cost controls supported by its new strategy, and the government’s €725 million multiannual funding commitment.

He said he would “appeal very strongly” for a similar multiannual commitment when it next comes for review.

When asked how much additional state funding RTÉ would be looking for from 2028, Bakhurst said discussions had not started.

He added: “We will need public funding. We will need funding from either the licence fee or a similar source of public funding.”

Woman's case about child sex abuse videos on porn sites adjourned over possible $120m settlement

The woman claims she was drugged and raped by a man when she was a child.

4.52pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

HIGH COURT PROCEEDINGS involving video companies behind Pornhub have been adjourned until March while a proposed $120 million (€105.5 million) settlement of US litigation awaits court approval.

The matter briefly came before Mr Justice Brian Cregan today, when counsel for the woman, identified as Jane Doe to protect her identity, requested an adjournment pending developments in the related US proceedings.

The woman, who lives in the United States, claims that she was drugged and raped by a man in the state of Alabama when she was sixteen years old.

She claims that her abuser recorded what happened and posted the images online.

It is alleged that videos of her abuse were published and distributed on various adult video sharing websites owned by the international group of companies that own, control and manage internet pornography websites including Pornhub.

The woman initially brought US proceedings against companies within the MindGeek group, the business behind Pornhub, which rebranded as Aylo in August 2023.

Those companies are MG Freesites Ltd, MG Freesites II Ltd, MindGeek SARL, Aylo Premium Ltd, MG Social Ltd, Mindgeek USA Incorporated, MG CY Holdings Ltd, Aylo Billing Ltd, Mirmay Ltd, Nutaku Publishing Ltd, Appatomic Ltd and Liquidim Ltd.

Five of those companies – Aylo Billing Ltd, Mirmay Ltd, Nutaku Publishing Ltd, Appatomic Ltd and Liquidum Ltd – are registered in Dublin.

Advertisement

She launched additional proceedings against those companies in Ireland’s High Court last year.

A US judge described the companies as a network that “own or operate several of the most-visited pornographic websites in the world”, including Pornhub, YouPorn, RedTube, Tube8 and WTube.

The settlement proposed in the US case would resolve class actions brought in the states of Alabama and California against the companies involved.

Pollock Cohen, one of the firms representing the plaintiffs, confirmed in August that the “historic” agreement would cover both cases and includes payments and changes to the websites’ practices. It remains subject to court approval.

The Irish proceedings, initiated due to the international structure of the defendant group, sought to preserve assets in Ireland while the US litigation progresses.

Aylo has said that the settlement involves no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement reported by the adult industry publication XBIZ, the company said that only verified creators can publish on its platform and that content uploaded to its websites undergoes technological checks and is reviewed by trained moderators before publication.

The Irish case reflects the international structure of the business and the woman’s efforts to pursue companies and assets across different jurisdictions.

The matter briefly came before the High Court today, when Judge Cregan adjourned the case until March at the request of the woman’s barrister Robert O’Reilly.

news.title: Criteria for Budget 2027's rural pub support scheme to be based on turnover
news.text:
In addition to the €15m fund to support pubs, the budget also allocated €3m for the establishment of the landmark Start Up Ireland initiative, €20m for the launch of the €500m Growth and Sustainability Loan Scheme, €4.5m for Local Enterprise Office, as well as €6.65m for Fáilte Ireland tourism product and destination development in the regions.

In addition, there was a €1bn Ireland’s Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) start-up and scaling investment programme announced for up to 2030. The funding will be in co-operation with Enterprise Ireland to provide a long-term source of capital for Irish scaling companies through equity and debt investments.

Other budget measures announced include an increase in the national minimum wage of 79c, an increase to PRSI thresholds, as well as a cut in the capital gain tax rate from 33% to 31%.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Mr Burke said the rural pubs are a “focal point for much of society to interact” and have been a “key area to combat social isolation”.

However, the number of rural pubs has been steadily shrinking. Rural Ireland has seen 2,200 pubs disappear since 2005. In Cork, there were 1,221 pubs in 2005, but in the two decades since it has fallen to 821.

Mr Burke said he plans to have the scheme ready for applicants by July 1 and he will be looking potentially having a “remit scheme which could most likely track the licences of publicans”.

"If you look at the licenses that are given out, there are a number of tiers or categories based on turnover, which dictate essentially what size the pub is,” he said.

"If you have [a pub] in the second tier, it's about €380,000 turnover,” he said, adding that roughly 70% of rural pubs are captured within that tier.

"I want to ensure that it is getting to our smaller type of publicans that are under pressure, that are facing very significant viability challenges. 

"A scheme will be crafted around that, looking at licensing laws, turnover, and also looking at environmental aid, how we make them more sustainable by encouraging the circular economy and recycling,” he said.

News of the support scheme was welcomed by the Vintners’ Federation of Ireland.

Minimum wage and PRSI

While the minister sold the budget as a pro-enterprise budget, the Small Firms Association (SFA) was critical of it, particularly the increase to the minimum wage which now sets it at €14.94.

To mitigate the rising minimum wage, the Government raised the employer threshold for PRSI from €552 to €600 per week.

However, the SFA had been seeking a temporary rebate on PRSI to help companies absorb the rising costs.

In response to this, Mr Burke said that firms will not be paying as much PRSI as they would have if it had tracked the increases in the minimum wage.

“That will help them a little bit. It's not going the full way but it is an assistance to dealing with the increase in the minimum wage,” he said.
news.summary: The €15m scheme is expected to open for applicants on July 1 next year

news.title: Celia Holman Lee experiences 'major health setback' and is receiving medical care
news.text: Celia Holman Lee has experienced a "major health setback" according to a statement shared on her social media. Taking to Instagram on Wednesday, her family shared a snap of the Irish fashion icon as they revealed she was receiving medical care. They wrote: “It is with heavy hearts that we share that Celia Holman Lee has experienced a major health setback and is currently receiving medical care. "As a result, Celia will be unavailable for public engagements for a period of time. Her family asks that their privacy be respected during this difficult period so that they can focus on her care and recovery. "The family is deeply grateful for the outpouring of love, prayers, and good wishes. Please know, that every message is appreciated and gives them strength. Given the volume of messages, they may not be able to respond individually, and ask for your understanding if they are unable to do so. "An update will be shared at an appropriate time. In the meantime, the family asks that all media respect their wishes.” Celia received an outpouring of kind words and well wishes from friends and followers, as one person commented: "Thoughts & prayers with you Celia & your lovely family." "Celia and family I am so sorry to hear this. I am sending prayers of health and healing to you," another said. A third wrote: "Wishing you strength Celia and sending love & prayers to your family." The news on her health comes just months after Celia opened up about how important is it to her to stay working and keep her mind active. "I work hard," she said. "I keep my mind active. I would say to any woman out there, if you retire... the mind is everything.... I watched one of my brothers. Leonard had very bad Alzheimer's and dementia. He was amazing. My father, Jackie, had it as well." Speaking to Evoke, she confirmed that the fears of not keeping her mind active with work is one of the reasons she has yet to retire. "I'd say it is," she said. "I have to because I know it is in the family. It's not like I'm running around the place. My daughter-in-law runs the agency now but I am at everything. I love it and I love people. "I do honestly feel keep your shoulders back and down, look after your appearance and keep active and you'll keep going." Want to see more of the stories you love from RSVP ? To add RSVP as a preferred source of news on Google, simply click here
news.summary: A statement has been shared on the social media of the Irish fashion icon as she will be unavailable for public engagements for the time being - her family have asked for privacy

news.title: Ben Kelliher goal decisive for Sem in O'Sullivan Cup semi
news.text:
St Brendan’s College were pushed all the way by a gusty Mercy Mounthawk side in this Kerry Colleges Senior Football (O’Sullivan Cup) semi-final played at the COE in Currans on a blustery afternoon.

St Brendan's were warm favourites but Mounthawk failed to read the script and powered by Ben Litchfield at midfield and hat-trick hero Mickey Somers on the forty, they were just two points adrift (2-12 to 3-7) with 10 minutes left.

Then St Brendan's College struck for the game-winning goal, when John Henderson, who had been introduced as a substitute, floated in a high ball that invited a classy flick over his head by Ben Kelliher to push the Killarney side five clear. The Sem embellished their margin with late points from Liam O’Brien, Mark O’Carroll and Finan Blackwell.

The opening half had been end to end stuff with 15-year-old Billy Kirby catching the eye for Mounthawk while Harry Murphy was combining well with Conor McGibney and Mikey Somers, under the watchful eye of his brother Ben, home from the AFL.

St Brenda'ns made the better start when Jake Coffey took advantage of a keeper error to finish to the Mounthawk net, while Mark O’Carroll, Cillian O’Donoghue and Jack Culloty added points.

After Rory Bowler opened the scoring for Mounthawk, Paddy Lucid sent Mikey Somers through and the St Senan's youngster buried the ball in the back of Sem net. Somers then levelled the contest with a two-point free but Kerry U-20 player Kelliher replied with an orange flag from play. 

The sides traded points before St Brendan’s struck for a second goal in the 19th minute, when Mark Looney intercepted a pass out of defence. He found Jack Culloty, who set up Kelliher, who finished clinically.

From the kickout, Mikey Somers took a two-point free that dropped under the crossbar to the net, to leave it 2-6 to 2-5 and game on.

Thanks to the foraging of Cian Stack, Jack Hallissey, Zach Cronin and Mark O’Carroll, St Brendan's tagged on three unanswered points from Kelliher, Daniel Cronin and Jack Culloty to retire 2-9 to 2-5 in front.

At the second throw-in, disaster struck Mounthawk, as towering midfielder Litchfield landed awkwardly on his ankle and had to retire.

Mounthawk did get another goal in the 39th minute, in bizarre fashion, when the referee moved a free into the 13 metre line and Mikey Somers, spotting the Sem defence had fallen asleep, fired to an unguarded net.

It was nip and tuck with Mounthawk kicking three bad wides before the St Brendan's captain Ben Kelliher decided the contest with that audacious 54th- minute goal.

 St Brendan's will now face either St Michaels College Listowel or Castleisland CC in a unique final.

 ST BRENDAN’S COLLEGE: J Casey (Spa); D McCarthy (Listry), Z Cronin (Kilcummin), C Clifford (Dr Crokes); C Lynch (Dr Crokes), C Stack (Kilcummin), J Hallissey (Fossa); M O’Carroll (Dr Crokes), J Coffey (Legion); M Looney (Legion), B Kelliher (Dr Crokes), D Cronin (Firies); L O’Brien (Glenflesk), C O’Donoghue (Listry), J Culloty (Legion).

 Subs: J Ahern (Kilcummin) for C Lynch (inj h/t), F Blackwell (Legion) for J Coffey (h/t), J Henderson (Firies) for C O’Donoghue (52), F O’Donnell (Dr Crokes) for L O’Brien (58), J Nash (Dr Crokes) for C Clifford (58).

 MERCY MOUNTHAWK: S Sargent (John Mitchels); C Nolan (Churchill), K O’Shea (Firies), E Crowley (Churchill); R Bowler (John Mitchels), C McGibney (Churchill), D Hobbert (Austin Stacks); B Litchfield (Austin Stacks), P Lucid (Austin Stacks); B Kirby (Austin Stacks), M Somers (St Senans), H Murphy (Austin Stacks); J Diggin (Austin Stacks), L O’Carroll (Churchill), R Onyekwere (Kerins O’Rahillys).

 Subs: J O’Dowd (Austin Stacks) for B Litchfield (inj 31), B Conway (John Mitchels) for J Diggin (43), M Carmody (Austin Stacks) for R Onyekwere (43).

 Referee: C O Dhúbhda (An Ghaeltacht).
news.summary: A classy goal by the the Kerry U20 star saw off a brave Mercy Mounthawk challenge

news.title: Cork City students champion country values in competition final
news.text:
The team, comprising Emma Dilworth, Meabh O’Donovan and Mary-Clare O’Connell, all come from farming backgrounds, with Ms O’Donovan and O’Connell hailing from dairy farms and Ms Dilworth coming from an organic beef farm. 

The team reached the final of this cycle of the competition with their project titled: ‘How organic farm practices can produce sustainable Certified Irish Angus beef’.

Discussing their initial interest in the competition, Ms O’Connell said: “We all come from farming backgrounds, but we have a huge interest in farming… We never ever thought it would take us here and we're so happy we entered.” 

The team’s project looked into researching organic farming practices and whether they could be incorporated into conventional farming systems, reducing emissions on farms, increasing biodiversity on farms through multispecies swards, and what effects it may have, the importance of beef in a diet and highlighting women in the agricultural industry.

Once reaching the final, the team were gifted their five cattle at the National Ploughing Championships last year. Housed on Ms O’Connell’s home farm, the cattle have become local celebrities dubbed “the Famous Five” by those who know them. The team were also lucky enough to secure a Dairygold sponsorship for their cattle meal.

Discussing how eye-opening and vital receiving the cattle were, the team said being able to apply knowledge collected at events or from speakers and researchers and to determine whether it could apply to their own cattle or help with improving their knowledge was invaluable.

“We had to think like the farmers,” Ms O’Donovan explained. “We can go to different events, and we can see and understand it, and that’s why having the cattle is so important,” Ms O‘Connell added.

The team, ever the advocates for their research, hosted a naming competition in their school, allowing the teachers to supply one name, the junior cycle supplied two and the senior cycle provided the remaining two. The cattle were subsequently christened: Bull McCabe, Rebel, Killeagh, Ferdinand and Cnoc.

The St Angela’s team all pitched in helping with the feed and upkeep of the Famous Five. The cattle were weighed every 100 days to monitor progress and were scheduled to go to the factory in August.

“It will be really sad to see them go… it was a great hands-on experience,” Ms Dilworth admitted.

Despite educating classmates on the realities from farm to fork, the team explained they were relieved the cattle were going to slaughter in August before school resumed so they could break the news gently to their fellow classmates.

“It’s a part of farming, and we will have to show them that part too,” Ms O’Connell said.

Through their advocacy and tireless work promoting and exposing their city-dwelling peers to a life of agriculture, the team have also boosted interest for St Angela's students to do agricultural science as a subject, with the school subsequently offering it on the curriculum for the first time last year instead of an after-school extra.

Alongside their teachers, Ms O’Donovan and Mr Barry-Murphy, a big supporter of the team's work was their principal and beef farmer, Mr Curran, who has provided a listening ear to the girls over any snags they came across with their project.

The team focused on multispecies swards, red clover, animal health and the environment as the main pillars of their research.

The cattle were monitored: they had faecal samples taken, and the results were then used to determine whether the animals were dosed for coccidiosis.

With their sponsorship from Grasstech and help from FBA Labs, the girls were able to compare organic multi-species sward growing on Ms Dilworth’s farm to conventional perennial-rye grass on Ms O’Connell’s farm, with the multi-species performing similarly to the conventional fertilised grass.

At FBA Labs, the team tested and compared silage samples between conventional silage and organic red clover silage. Through their trials, they found on conventional silage their cattle were putting on 0.4kg/day, but on organic red clover silage they were putting on double at 0.8kg/day.

With their trials, the girls also visually observed more pollinators and biodiversity with the multi-species swards when compared to conventional.

The team contacted local organic farmers, and under the guidance of Kay O’Sullivan, who farms an organic beef suckler and sheep farm out in Mourneabbey in Cork, she was able to offer insight into organics and educate them on soil testing.

Reaching out to other influential women in agriculture, the team spoke with Katherine O’Leary from the Irish Farmers Journal, who offered advice to the team, who described Ms O’Leary as a “trailblazer” and “mentor” in helping to navigate their project. 

The team also met with Aileen Sheehan, a local teacher and farmer who won FBD Young Farmer of the Year in 2025 as the first woman to win the award, with the team crediting her as a “great inspiration” for them.

While the research focused on biodiversity, animal health, grass growth and nutrition, the students said the biggest lesson they learned was that organic and conventional farming are not as far apart as many people believe.

Throughout the project, the team worked to challenge misconceptions among both farmers and consumers, arguing sustainability does not have to come at the expense of productivity.

For the St Angela's team, it was never about encouraging every farmer to convert to a fully organic system. Instead, they hoped to show small, practical changes could make a meaningful difference on farms of all types.

Their central message is one they hope farmers, consumers and policymakers alike take on board.

 Organic farming is not a million miles away. It’s tangible, it’s achievable, it’s important, it’s sustainable, and it’s economical.

Looking back on nearly three years of research, farm visits, presentations and caring for their “Famous Five” cattle, the students believe the future of Irish farming will involve adopting sustainable practices that work alongside existing systems rather than replacing them entirely.

It is a conclusion backed by the team's research as part of the competition and one they hope will encourage more farmers to see sustainability not as a challenge to their businesses, but as an opportunity to strengthen them for the future.
news.summary: Kicking off our five-part series, we take a look at the team from St Angela's College located in Cork City who are finalists of the Certified Irish Angus Schools Competition

Raised in Turner's Cross and built on the road - the faces and places that made Ireland's Megan Connolly

The 42 sits down with Luke and Michael Connolly to discuss the rise of Megan in professional football.

4.47pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Sinead Farrell

IT’S COMING TO the end of a Munster senior cup final in Cork, and the manager of one of the teams is facing a selection dilemma.

Michael Connolly, who established the women’s section of College Corinthians AFC, is already down to his sub keeper in a 2-2 battle. They’re up against fierce rivals, and defending champions, Wilton United. 

His replacement keeper is pulling off the saves and keeping them in the fight as the game enters extra time. But with neither side looking likely to nab a winner, she comes to Connolly with a crisis of confidence.

“I’m not going in goals for the penalties,” she says.

“Not a bother,” Michael replies with reassurance. “I’ve a plan.”

Megan Connolly pictured in the goalkeeper jersey celebrating with her Corinthians team.Luke Connolly

Luke Connolly

Connolly’s daughter Megan is also a player on the Corinthians team. In truth, he built this team for her when he saw she had a flair for the sport. He canvassed schools. He put up flyers. The whole family helped put the work in to assemble a team. All in the hope that Megan could take her passion further when there were no other opportunities around the Douglas area.

Megan normally plays up front and has provided both of her side’s goals in this game in Charleville. Megan is also a Chelsea fan. Moreover, she’s a hardcore Petr Čech worshipper. She even has a pair of gloves that are similar to the ones he plays with. And now she’s going to get her chance to emulate her idol.

Michael has faith, despite her lack of match experience between the sticks. He knows that she’s good at reading what direction a shooter will aim for.

Megan uses those instincts to save all three of Wilton’s penalties as Corinthians are crowned the new champions. But when it comes to naming the Player of the Match, Megan Connolly is not selected for the award.

Walking out from the pitch, Michael runs into the official who is responsible for this decision. 

“Look, Megan has a load of them, I’d say,” he says, offering his apologies.

“That’s not the point,” comes Michael’s reply.

“The point is that she scored two goals, she saved the penalties, and she was deserving of it. That’s it.”

Michael is recalling Megan’s recent graduation as he sits down to tea with his son, Luke. His son has just moved into a new house in Innishannon, so they’re sipping from disposable cups for the moment. Thankfully, he’s not straying too far from home where he played football for Nemo Rangers and Cork. His playing days are over, but he’s still involved with the Nemo seniors as a coach.

There are some odd jobs left to be done to help Luke settle in with his family. His young son, Shea, has just come home from crèche. Life is blissfully busy.

But they can spare some time to talk about Megan, the youngest of the three siblings. Luke is the eldest, and they have another sister, Nicole.

Megan’s graduation was in London where she picked up a diploma in Global Football Business Management. Australian legend Tim Cahill was also receiving a qualification that day along with former Chelsea star César Azpilicueta.

Megan was especially happy to see him there.

Megan was a big Chelsea and Petr Čech fan growing up.Luke Connolly.

Luke Connolly.

But for Michael and his wife, Freda, the biggest shock was seeing their youngest speak on stage for 10 minutes about her course.

“She never told us that she was being interviewed on stage. To be honest, you can never tell with Megan.”

A new person stood before them compared to the girl they raised in Cork. She’s done a lot of growing up since moving to Florida State University in 2015 on a four-year scholarship as a teenager.

The next four years were spent at Brighton & Hove Albion in the Women’s Super League [WSL], before a brief stint at Bristol City. She’s now into her third year as a Serie A player with Lazio.

All that moving around has altered her accent slightly. Luke is waiting for an Italian flavour to show up in her “mid-Atlantic” twang, but Michael assuredly says that there’s still some Cork in there.

Megan Connolly [right] in action for Lazio.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

“She rings me and goes, ‘Hello, Boyyyyy.’ She’d be mocking me then.”

Freda has remarked in the past how Megan went to Florida as a shy girl, and came home a confident woman. Luke agrees with that observation.

“The Megan that left wouldn’t be the same Megan that captained a WSL team. She’s become more of a leader.”

And as she prepares to turn 30 next year, with 70 Ireland caps banked, she’s looking to the future and the life that awaits after playing professional football.

“She’s looked at what would keep her interested in soccer,” Michael explains. “Coaching is one thing, but then there’s other backroom things that she’d like to get into. From being in the States when she was 18 to now where she’s 29. So over that 11 years, she’s been in and out of the Irish team, and she’s had different experiences.”

The machine wouldn’t accept Michael’s match ticket, and he couldn’t understand why. It was a rainy night in June, and he was trying to get into the Premium Level of Páirc Uí Chaoimh to watch Megan play for Ireland in their World Cup qualifier against the Netherlands. 

Luke had no trouble getting through, and was sinking into some pints with his work colleagues before kick-off. It was a breeze for Nicole and her family too.

But their father was having some technical difficulties. The machine kept popping his ticket back out to him. A friendly steward stepped in to provide assistance, and kindly pointed out that he was in the wrong section of the stadium.

“I was down in the front with the rain,” Michael laughs. “There were a few girls there who work with Freda and they always support Megan. And they were like, ‘Where’s everyone else?’ And I was pointing up to where they were.”

But missing out on the Premium Level luxuries proved to be no loss in the end for Michael. Ireland kept their automatic World Cup qualification hopes alive that night with a dramatic 3-2 victory. Amber Barrett provided the match-winner in the 90th minute, and Michael had the best view in the house.

Advertisement

Michael Connolly was sitting right in front of the celebrations after Amber Barrett's winner against the Netherlands.Ben Brady / INPHO

Ben Brady / INPHO / INPHO

“I was right in front of where Amber celebrated the third goal,” he continued.

“It was great because I got down to Megan for a hug. I wouldn’t have got that, so it worked out well.”

The Ireland women’s team have enjoyed some famous results at Páirc Uí Chaoimh in recent years. It’s quickly becoming their favourite venue. Along with that massive result against the Dutch, you can also add a 1-0 win over Slovenia from the 2025 Nations League to the list.

It all started in 2024, with a 3-1 result against France to mark their first win of their Euro 2025 qualification campaign. It was also Ireland’s first senior women’s home international outside of Dublin since June 2012.

Megan came on in the last few minutes, and sent in a corner for Anna Patten to score Ireland’s third goal of the game. But for the Connollys, there were some challenging emotions to work through during that game.

“She did some of the media before the game but she almost didn’t feature,” Luke begins. “She came on, took a corner, and they got the third goal. That put a positive spin on what would have been a fairly disastrous trip to Cork for us. She just wasn’t getting in under Eileen (Gleeson). But that’s our hit.

“There was huge support there. There were 300 girls down there who wanted to run out onto the pitch after the game. There’s that part of it as well.

“That’s what you sometimes don’t appreciate. From canvassing the schools to winning in Cork in front of girls. Maybe we don’t appreciate that side of it enough.”

Megan Connolly in action at Páirc Uí Chaoimh.Ben Brady / INPHO

Ben Brady / INPHO / INPHO

The Connollys have followed Megan’s Ireland career closely, even when they couldn’t watch her play. In the days before TV coverage, they only had an FAI stream to rely on that didn’t have any live actual footage of the game.

“We remember watching the bar like a Football Manager game,” Luke explains. “If we were attacking, it would go green. We’d just keep watching the bar and if they missed a chance, we’d be like, ‘Oh, fuck sake.’ So, it’s nice to actually watch games instead of making up scenarios in our head.”

They feel all the bad moments with Megan, as much as the good ones. On the night Ireland secured World Cup qualification in 2022, Megan was at home with her family. They were all together for Amber Barrett’s famous winning goal against Scotland at Hampden Park.

A surreal memory. They knew Megan should be playing, but was unavailable due to a serious injury. Two fractured ribs and a grade three laceration of the kidney forced her to watch the drama unfold on TV.

Luke was still playing for Nemo Rangers in those days, and missed the first half of the game due to training. Someone kept him informed of the updates before he could get home to watch the second half.

In 2021, during another World Cup qualifier against Sweden, Luke used a different method to stay informed.

“We watched the first half, and then I had training. We were getting ready for a [championship] semi-final, and I had the phone in my sock.” 

Of course, the Connollys all flew out to Australia too for the tournament itself. A historic occasion for Irish football and a career highlight for Megan. The first group game against the host nation, Australia, was almost overwhelming for Luke.

“We were definitely emotional when they were walking out because it’s kind of like a ‘She did it’ moment.”

It’s about a week into Megan Connolly’s transfer to Lazio, and she wants to come home. This is her third club as a professional footballer, but it’s not her first experience with homesickness.

She was struck down with a bout of it during her final years at Florida State as her role in the team gradually changed from influential leader to impact player.

Now she’s showing symptoms again as she tries to adjust to life in Italy. She’s used to certain training methods from her time with Brighton and Bristol in the Women’s Super League.

But it’s different in Lazio. They use old-school training methods. It’s an all-male coaching staff too.

The heat doesn’t make it any easier. It’s 40 degrees outside and Megan’s accommodation doesn’t have any air conditioning.

Megan Connolly was captain of Brighton during her time there.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Megan’s mother, Freda, sobbed for weeks when her youngest left the house to go to Florida for four years. But in these moments of doubt, she’s the one that says what her daughter needs to hear.

“You’ve signed a contract. You have to honour it.”

It gets easier for Megan as the weeks go by. She checks herself into a hotel for a month to catch up on some sleep in an air-conditioned room. Within a month, she’s in a beautiful apartment. She then makes her first start at centre-back against Roma. The perfect tonic for a bad case of homesickness. 

“When you’re playing well, stuff like that tends to fade a bit,” Luke explains. “She’s at the point now where they’ve had girls come over, and she can see if they’ll last because it is such a culture shock.

“In Brighton, the training facilities are top class. Lazio have improved and have their own facilities. But if the men’s team have to go out on the pitch, they’ll (the women’s team) be demoted to the (other pitch). Because it’s so hot in Italy this month, they actually train on astroturf.

“So, there’s still a bit of an old-school approach there. And in pre-season, they’re running. There’s no footballs.”

The Connolly home lies in the shadow of two great stadiums in Cork. Turner’s Cross is their address, not far from the home ground of Cork City. It was a regular haunt for the Connollys when the children were young.

The home games they attended in 2005 were particularly memorable as Cork City edged out Derry City to win the Premier Division. Their title race went to the final day when Damien Richardson’s side earned a 2-0 win over the Candystripes at a packed-out Turner’s Cross to secure a first Premier Division title since 1993.

Páirc Uí Chaoimh, the headquarters of Cork GAA, is the other major sporting venue within reach of the Connolly household. Visits to Páirc Uí Chaoimh would come in later years for the Connollys. Luke’s career with the Cork footballers, combined with county final appearances for Nemo Rangers, has given them plenty of days out.

That could have been Megan’s life too. She also played for Nemo Rangers and represented Cork up to the U16 grade before she was prompted to make a decision. An All-Ireland final against Galway was clashing with a match for Ireland, and the message relayed to her father was clear.

Megan played centre for for Nemo Rangers. She's pictured second from the left on the bottom row here.

“If she doesn’t come to Dublin, she can play Gaelic for the rest of her life.”

“And I said to her, ‘You’ve got to do one or the other.’”

Michael is certain that a future in a Cork jersey was there for her. Centre-forward was her best position, and she was a dominant force in that sport too.

“I remember when she was 14, 15, they brought out a rule in Cork of one hop, one solo, and you had to get rid of the ball then. Because certain girls would just run through the whole place.

“So I said to Megan, ‘Just throw it on the floor and go with it and dribble through.’

“We played a club in Cork and the manager was running onto the pitch shouting, ‘She can’t do that!’”

Soccer won her heart and brought her down a different road. But she would eventually find herself at the gates of Páirc Uí Chaoimh too.

When they were young, the back garden was the preferred venue for the Connolly kids. Matches. Kicking drills. Basically, anything that involved ball work would keep them out on the grass for hours.

“There’s plants that can speak for the amount of games we had at home,” Luke recalls. “The remnants of tomato trees. Glass houses that didn’t last too long.” 

Nicole would normally retire after a match that was up to five goals. That left Luke and Megan to play on. The new target would be best of 50. Last one left standing. Their battles could go on until nightfall.

At that point, Michael would be pleading with them to come inside.

A young Megan Connolly in her Corinthians gear.Luke Connolly.

Luke Connolly.

“I would be saying to Luke, ‘Just leave her win.’ And then at about six o’clock, Megan would come in with the chest out. ’27-26. I just won.’”

But those victories weren’t built on any appeals for leniency. Luke could see that she was getting stronger with every game, and could do little to stop her.

“There’s four years between us, but it wasn’t too long where I was like, ‘I’m not letting her fucking win.’”

The garden is also where both Megan and Luke became dead-ball specialists. Luke could kick frees off the ground in Gaelic football, while Megan learned to become proficient at swinging in corners as well as hooking frees around a wall of defenders.

A famous example is from the U19 European Championships in 2014. Ireland, who were appearing at the competition for the first time, were 1-1 with Sweden in a group game when Connolly stood over a free with 10 minutes to go. With the aid of the crossbar, she knocked it into the top corner to send Ireland into the semi-finals.

FAI TV / YouTube

(Skip to 1:05 for Connolly’s match-winning free)

Her corners are a staple for Ireland. Both arms raised before applying the whip is the typical routine. Her delivery in the 89th minute of Ireland’s win over France in 2024 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh is an important one to note. Connolly left her mark on the pitch that’s close to home, using the tricks her father taught her.

“Frees and corners were a family thing,” Luke says. “The reason he taught us was basically, ‘If you’re having a bad game, give them a reason not to take you off.’ I don’t think it really happened with Megan, but if there ever was a day when you were having a bad game, you could say, ‘Yeah, but we need her for the corners.’ 

“It’s a key part of her Irish career.”

Megan was always a quiet player on the field. Hardly a word, according to Michael. And not very expressive either. She never broke into wild or excessive celebrations after a goal. Never goaded an opponent when she was dominating a game.

That was an important quality when she was such a formidable presence on the field. Her gamesmanship earned her a lot of respect as she progressed from Corinthians to Florida State. Her international career started by making an U15 squad. In 2014, she was on that Ireland U19 side at the European Championships.

It was packed with future greats of women’s sport. Sarah Rowe, a current star of the AFLW, was involved as was Cork camogie All-Ireland winner Amy O’Connor. Katie McCabe and Chloe Mustaki were there too, and still share an Ireland dressing room with Megan.

Luke had a different personality on the field. His father laughs in agreement, and follows it up with a story to illustrate the difference between his two children.

Luke Connolly captained Nemo Rangers to Cork senior glory in 2022.Lorraine O’Sullivan / INPHO

Lorraine O’Sullivan / INPHO / INPHO

The scene is the 2020 Cork premier senior football final – played in 2021 due to Covid – between Nemo Rangers and their rivals Castlehaven. Luke has just scored his second goal to help seal a 3-7 to 0-13 victory. He raises his arms to the crowd in celebration before dropping a finger to his lips, shushing the Castlehaven supporters.

The Connolly men take up the story.

“His mother was saying, ‘What’s he doing?’ And I says, ‘He’s not doing what he’s supposed to be doing.’ He ran across jeering them.”

Luke laughs as he interjects.

“I don’t think that’s accurate now. They were calling me names.” 

Another visit to Páirc Uí Chaoimh awaits for Ireland. And the Connollys. As the World Cup qualification journey continues against Kazakhstan, the venue where they have a 3-0 record was the only place that could host such a crucial fixture. The first leg of the play-off is coming up this Friday in Astana Arena before Carla Ward’s side return to the banks of the Lee on Tuesday, 13 October.

Another homecoming of sorts for Megan and her lifelong friend, Denise O’Sullivan. An image of the Cork comrades in their Ireland shirts is immortalised in a traffic box mural in the city. A fitting dedication to their legacy. 

Come On You Girls In Green! 

Our new traffic box mural at South Gate Bridge in @corkcitycentre dedicated to Cork's Megan Connolly and Denise O'Sullivan who will be bringing home the @FIFAWomensWorl3 Cup later this summer for @FAIWomen https://t.co/RR9LoZBA8J— People's Republic of Cork (@cork) May 26, 2023

“She’s always had Megan’s back,” Luke adds. “If Megan’s not playing, she’d be saying, ‘You should be playing, girl.’”

The Connollys will also be in Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday, 10 October in their Nemo Rangers colours for a senior football semi-final against Carrigaline. Luke is part of the backroom team these days. He stopped playing in 2023 with five senior county medals and two Munster crowns to his name. They’ve lost the last three county finals, but he’s hoping for a different ending this year.

“I have a jersey for Shea. We have a family photo from last year which is the first time that the three generations were there. It would be nice to win one as a coach.”

Lots to look forward to in the next few weeks just down the road from where it all started in Turner’s Cross.

“You still think it’s going to disappear in the morning. If anything happened, she’s had such a career. She’s been through Florida State, Brighton, Bristol, World Cup, Lazio.

“When we were canvassing in school, you’d be saying, ‘Remember now, this is all for you.’”

news.title: ‘Lean review’ of DAFM TB programme to continue in 2027
news.text:
A 'lean review' of the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine's bovine tuberculosis (TB) programme is set to continue next year.

As part of Budget 2027, government departments have been asked to deliver efficiencies and reforms. 

Among the measures highlighted by DAFM was the continuation of its lean review of the bovine TB programme across all Regional Veterinary Offices (RVO).

DAFM said this will help to identify "increased efficiencies in the operation of the programme".

"This will continue across all areas of the programme throughout 2027 to enforce the building of a Lean culture across the BTB programme," the department added.

Under Budget 2027, DAFM has been allocated €142.4 million for the TB programme for next year.

This is around €15 million less than the allocation for the programme for this year (2026), which was €157 million.

The department is expecting to carry out some 10.7 million bovine TB tests on cattle next year.

It has also been confirmed that the existing valuation ceilings will increase by €500 for all reactor animals valued in 2026.

Among the other efficiencies highlighted by DAFM was the strategic deployment of artifical intelligence (AI) "to drive business value and innovation". 

The department plans to continue developing AI pathfinder projects which could "deliver administration efficiencies to our staff and better serve our customers".

This may include reducing the time to write documents and process applications. 

The department said it will ensure staff have "appropriate training and skills to use AI responsibly and effectively".

DAFM also said it reuses and extends existing technology wherever possible to "maximise value, accelerate delivery, and achieve both time and cost efficiencies". 

It said that spatial analysis capabilities originally developed for forestry schemes have been repurposed to support work on appropriate assessments under the nitrates derogation.

Food controls

In July 2024, the government announced the phased transfer of the official food controls undertaken by local authority veterinary services from the Department of Health (DoH) to DAFM. 

This includes the permanent transfer of funding and the transfer of relevant staff from local authorities to DAFM effective from January 1, 2027.

The department said that it will be more efficient both from an operational and financial perspective to absorb the functions into DAFM’s laboratory complex in Co Kildare.

The department also confirmed that it will carry out a "critical review" of the EU School Fruit and Vegetables and School MilkSchemes ahead of changes to the relevant EU regulations in 2028. 

These schemes are currently cofinanced by EU and national exchequer funding.

The objective of the review will be to simplify and better align these schemes with the Hot School Meals Scheme.

As part of Budget 2027, government departments have been asked to deliver efficiencies and reforms. news.title: Tesco looking for new sites for Express chain of stores
news.text:
Tesco confirmed the opening to the Irish Examiner, saying the outlet will open at the end of November and employ 15 people. "As our third Express store opening this year, it will bring the total number of Tesco Express stores across Ireland to 62," a spokesperson said.

Tesco, currently Ireland's second-largest supermarket chain after Dunnes Stores, already operates a full supermarket in Ballincollig. 

It opened another outlet on Cork's South Main Street in 2024, but the company said it is seeking other locations suitable to open further stores.

"We have ambitious plans to continue growing our convenience store network and are actively looking for suitable sites nationwide. 

"We are particularly interested in units of 3,000 sq ft and above, located on busy roads, high streets, or within established retail locations. Both leasehold and freehold opportunities will be considered," the company said.

Tesco has a 24% market share of Ireland's grocery sector. The British chain is led by Cork-born chief executive Ken Murphy.

Publishing results in June, the company said sales in Ireland had grown 5.56% to £838m (€966m), boosted by strong growth in food sales and online shopping.

In July, it was reported that the company was considering the sale of its operations in Central Europe in order to focus on the UK and Ireland.

Discount retailer EuroGiant closed its outlet at Ballincollig's Eastside Centre earlier this year, having opened at the site. The location was previously occupied by supermarket chain Iceland before its exit from the Irish market.
news.summary: British supermarket giant to open new Ballincollig outlet in November
news.author: Alan Healy,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Ornua PPI indicative milk price up 2c/L
news.text:
The Ornua Purchase Price Index (PPI) has increased for September, resulting in an indicative milk price increase of 2c/L.

The PPI for September is 135.8, an increase of the previous month's index of 130.4.

Ornua said this implies an indicative return of 38.2c/L, including 4.5% VAT, for milk at 3.6% fat and 3.3% protein.

This is an increase on the return for August of 36.2c/L, and is net of Ornua's costs to market.

The price is derived from deducting estimated processing costs for Ornua's member processors. This cost stood at 10c/L for September.

The estimated processing cost is based on Ornua’s estimate of the average cost of processing the Ornua "basket of products", which is not representative of any of Ornua's individual member processors.

The estimated processing cost does not include any allowance for member processor margin, and is based on external indices of variable costs (most importantly energy).

The estimated processing cost can increase or decrease every quarter of the year, depending on movements in those external indices.

Ornua said the latest PPI and indicative milk price return "reflect stronger market returns for the month of September".

However, Ornua also said that the PPI does not directly align with milk production and payments, for "reasons of seasonality".

In other dairy market news, the Global Dairy Trade (GDT) index has increased following the latest trading event held this week.

The index has increased by 1.2% to 1,177 as a result of the auction which took place yesterday (Tuesday, October 6).

The result reverses the impact of a 1.1% fall in the index after the last trading event in mid September.

This week's event saw a total of 41,692t of dairy commodities traded with an average winning price of $3,928/t.

The results show a mixed picture when it comes to movement in the average prices for each of the product sub-indices.

The index for skim milk powder (SMP) rose by 4.3% to an average price of $3,847/t.

Whole milk powder (WMP) was up 1.2% to an average of $3,605/t, while butter milk powder rose by 0.7% to $4,123/t.

However, there was a 6.9% fall in the average price of lactose to $1,677/t.

Cheddar was back 3.7% to $3,925/t and mozzarella decreased by 3.9% to $3,833/t.

There was a slight fall (-0.3%) for butter to leave an average price of $4,740/t, while anhydrous milk fat was down by 1.1% to $5,683/t.
