news.title: Turkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis
news.text:
Turkey is sending mainly defensive and ​technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, two officials said on Wednesday, ‌after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to act on the collective defence commitment of their newly formed alliance.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member constituted an attack on all. They have been working ​to set the parameters of the new alliance and have held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.

On ​Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defence ⁠commitments and ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a ​robust defence industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh’s technical military needs, and agreed ​to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the support expected from Turkey was only in the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had ​taken place as part of the alliance so far.

DRONE OPERATORS, FINE-TUNING DEFENSIVE MEASURES

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan attends the Mecca defense pact meeting between Turkey, Saudi Arabia ​and Pakistan in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 5, 2026. Saudi Press Agency/Handout via REUTERS Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

Officials have said that Turkish support for Saudi ​Arabia — including air defence systems — would largely be in a bilateral capacity for now, as Turkey’s parliament has not officially ratified the joint pact. ‌The amount ⁠and nature of the support would increase after ratification, they have said.

A US official briefed on the matter said that Turkey had so far decided to send capabilities that were broadly defensive, including strategic planning support and help with logistics. The official said the assistance included drone operators and help with fine-tuning defensive measures, as well as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

Turkish Foreign ​Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking to ​state media after an extraordinary ⁠meeting of the Mecca alliance in Riyadh, said the sides had discussed what support to provide Saudi Arabia to help its defensive capabilities.

“We had our Defence Minister and Chief of ​General Staff with us, and they especially provided very fruitful views on military issues, operational ​issues, and technical ⁠matters,” he said on Monday.

Pakistani and regional officials have said Ankara and Islamabad have provided Saudi Arabia with military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen.

This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near ⁠the Bab ​el-Mandeb Strait, an international shipping route for energy exports and other trade.

Officials ​had told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning an offensive against the Houthis, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red ​Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts.

Source: Reuters
news.summary: Turkey is sending mainly defensive and ​technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, two officials said on Wednesday, ‌after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to act on the collective defence commitment of their newly formed alliance. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, […]

news.title: New Maltese historical novel brings sixteenth-century Birgu to life before the Great Siege
news.text:
Maltese author Stephen Magri will publish his debut historical novel, Thumasi Zahra - A Soul Taught Mercy Before the Great Siege, as an eBook on 9 October 2026.

Set principally in sixteenth-century Birgu in the years before the Great Siege of 1565, the novel approaches one of Malta’s most familiar historical periods from an unusual direction: through the lives of ordinary people before the siege itself begins.

At the centre of the story is Thumasi Zahra, the son of a harbour labourer. Growing up among dockworkers, galleys, captives, noble households and the Knights of St John, Thumasi discovers an unusual gift for languages. That ability gradually draws him beyond the world into which he was born and brings him into contact with people of very different rank and experience.

Yet the novel is concerned as much with conscience as with history. Thumasi is raised in a deeply Catholic household and learns early that mercy is easier to praise than to practise. As a child, troubled by the sight of chained captives in the harbour, he begins asking questions for which the adults around him do not always have comfortable answers.

His parish priest later teaches him the words Manus Christi — “the hands of Christ” — an idea that remains with him: faith does not remove the obligation to act, and mercy may have to work through ordinary human hands.

As Thumasi grows older, his life becomes increasingly entangled with a noble household and with Lucia di Santocanale, a young woman whose social world is closed to him by class and family expectation. Their growing attachment develops quietly against the rigid distinctions of sixteenth-century society and the hostility of Lucia’s brother.

The story also brings Thumasi into the orbit of the Knights of St John. Training, harbour work and an episode at sea force him to confront the difference between courage and violence, while the political and military pressures surrounding Malta begin to gather in the background.

Rather than treating the years before the Great Siege merely as a prelude to battle, Thumasi Zahra seeks to recreate Birgu as a lived place: its streets, harbour, churches, households, work, social divisions and moral tensions.

“Malta’s history is often told through commanders, battles and fortifications,” Magri said. “I wanted to look at the same world from below — through a family that works, worries, prays and tries to live decently while larger historical forces are beginning to move around them.”

The novel is the first volume of the planned Thumasi Zahra trilogy.
news.summary: Maltese author Stephen Magri will publish his debut historical novel, Thumasi Zahra - A Soul Taught Mercy Before the Great Siege, as an eBook on 9 October 2026

news.title: WATCH | Moroccan community, friends bid emotional farewell to murder victim Abdellatif Oumakhlouf
news.text:
There was little that needed to be said when the coffin holding Abdellatif Oumakhlouf's body was brought outside. Placed beside the wall outside the mortuary, it was surrounded by the people who had come to say goodbye to the young man who was murdered in Paceville.

Members of Malta’s Moroccan community, friends, his uncle, and colleagues from Attard Brothers, where he worked, gathered in prayer, standing around the coffin before it began its final journey home. Oumakhlouf's body will be taken back to his family in Morocco.

The gathering on Wednesday was marked by grief, but also by solidarity. Among those present was Dounia Borg, the president of the Morroccan community in Malta, who has been closely involved in the efforts surrounding the body's repatriation. She thanked members of the Moroccan community and the victim’s friends for coming together, as well as everyone who helped make it possible for his body to be returned to his family.

She expressed particular gratitude towards the Moroccan representative in Rome for the assistance provided throughout the process. In a moment shaped both by faith and tradition, Borg explained that the prayers around the coffin were attended by the men of the community.

But beyond the formalities of repatriation, Wednesday’s farewell became something more personal; an opportunity for those who knew him to speak about the man behind the tragedy.

Oumakhlouf's uncle struggled with emotion as he described his nephew simply as a good young man—someone who did not go looking for trouble. He also thanked Malta’s Moroccan community for the support it had offered the family throughout the ordeal, saying that what had been achieved would not have been possible without the people who came together to help.

For a family grieving from another country, that community became the hands on the ground in Malta—helping to ensure that their loved one could finally be brought home.

A close friend of the victim was equally emotional. He described Oumakhlouf as a person without malice, someone he remembered simply as a very good human being.

And behind the life he had built in Malta, his friend said, was a personal ambition; he wanted to help his family. That was what he had been working towards, the friend said.

Oumakhlouf's employer spoke with the same sense of loss. “We lost one of our family,” the Attard Brothers representative said. “We are a family here and we will miss him.”

The words captured what was visible outside the mortuary—people who crossed Oumakhlouf's path converging in one place to bid him farewell him. And as Malta prepares to return him to the home he had hoped to support, those who had become his community here came together for one final act of friendship.

On Friday, Oumakhlouf's body is expected to be back in Morocco, where his family will finally be able to receive him and lay him to rest.

The farewell ceremony comes little more than a week after Oumakhlouf, 31, was found dead at Spinola Gardens in St Julian’s following an early-morning altercation.

Police investigations, aided by CCTV footage from the surrounding area, led to the arrest of 27-year-old Polish tourist Sebastian Malinowski. He has since been charged with Oumakhlouf’s wilful homicide and grievous bodily harm resulting in death, charges to which he has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody while the case continues before the courts.
news.summary: Friends, relatives, colleagues and members of Malta’s Moroccan community gathered in prayer at the hospital mortuary on Wednesday to give murder victim Abdellatif Oumakhlouf a dignified send-off • 'We lost one of our family'
news.author: Jaelle Borg

news.title: Paramount-Warner Bros merger – How the deal could affect you
news.text:
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.

The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.

Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do – from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.

Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.

1. Streaming prices may rise

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.

Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers’ wallets over time.

While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.

The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.

Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come.

While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that “it’s far-fetched to think it’ll prevent downstream price hikes”.

2. More film releases

As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.

For the first two years, that’s 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.

That’s 156 movies in total – and the majority have to be “wide releases,” meaning they must be shown in cinemas.

The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.

If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.

Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.

“Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility,” she said.

“Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift”.

Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.

As Disney’s $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.

Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.

3. Hollywood jobs could be hit

For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a “disaster” by those on the ground.

Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.

Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was “heartbroken”.

“It’s people that make this city,” she said. “It’s people that make entertainment, it’s the everyday creatives that this industry is built on – this is who it hurts.”

A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.

The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.

Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that “it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities”.

She warned that Hollywood may become less of a “single location” and more of a “dispersed network.”

Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.

“Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs,” attorney Gilliam added.

4. CNN and CBS could change

To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.

The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure – CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump – as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson – the former director general of the BBC – to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News’s editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.

Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.

Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as “worthless”.

“The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news,” Stern said.

Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. “An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation,” she said.

Read more via BBC
news.summary: It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance. Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business […]

news.title: Centric and Talexio partner to connect Odoo ERP with Maltese payroll platform
news.text:
Malta-based technology company Centric has partnered with HR and payroll platform Talexio to integrate Odoo ERP with Talexio’s payroll software, giving businesses a new way to connect their enterprise resource planning and payroll systems.

Odoo is an all-in-one business management platform that brings functions including accounting, sales, purchasing, inventory and other business operations together in a single system. The new integration allows Odoo users to connect their existing setup with Talexio payroll, creating a smoother flow of payroll-related data between the two platforms.

For businesses seeking a payroll solution built around Maltese requirements, Talexio combines local payroll expertise with its HR and payroll platform. The integration allows companies to add Talexio payroll to an existing Odoo environment without having to create a separate manual process for transferring information.

Instead of exporting data, re-entering it and checking it before each payroll run, organisations can transfer information between the two systems with minimal intervention. This removes the need for double data entry, reduces the risk of errors during data transfer and means businesses do not have to migrate existing payroll records from Talexio to Odoo.

"At Centric, we believe technology should work around the business, not the other way around," said Kieran Sant, CEO of Centric. "By connecting Odoo with Talexio, businesses can keep the payroll system they already know and trust while removing the manual work between the two platforms. It’s a simple integration, but one that can make a real difference to day-to-day operations."

Businesses can configure the integration according to their own processes. Data can be transferred automatically through an application programming interface, or API, or exported as a structured Excel file for teams that prefer to review information before it reaches payroll.

Transfers can also be scheduled around regular payroll cycles or triggered manually when required. This gives businesses the flexibility to support highly automated payroll processes while also allowing organisations to retain a review step where needed.

Mark Camilleri Gambin, CEO and co-founder of Talexio, said the integration gives clients greater flexibility in how they manage their systems.

"This integration brings a great level of flexibility for our clients," he said. "Odoo provides a robust ERP foundation, while Talexio ensures payroll can be processed accurately, on time and in line with the relevant legislation. By connecting the two systems, businesses can avoid manual processes and create a smoother flow of information between their ERP and payroll. This supports our mission to improve employee and organisational wellbeing by removing unnecessary friction from everyday operations."

The partnership brings together Centric’s expertise in Odoo implementation and integrations with Talexio’s experience in HR and payroll technology. Centric supports businesses across Malta with Odoo implementation, system customisation, data migration, training and ongoing local support.

Talexio supports more than 2,000 organisations and has more than 27,000 active users on its HR platform. Its modular system covers core HR, time and attendance, performance management and payroll, allowing organisations to use the modules they need and integrate them with other business systems.

The company’s payroll software processes more than 34,500 payslips each month and is designed around Maltese tax, social security and statutory requirements. The platform combines local payroll expertise with a flexible HR system that can be integrated into a company’s wider technology environment.

The new Odoo-Talexio integration gives businesses a practical way to connect two systems they already rely on, reducing manual processes while keeping payroll within a platform tailored to the Maltese market.
news.summary: Malta-based technology company Centric partners with HR and payroll platform Talexio to integrate Odoo ERP with Talexio’s payroll software, giving businesses a new way to connect their enterprise resource planning and payroll systems
news.author: Staff Reporter

news.title: Malta registers Europe’s largest annual increase in tourism GDP contribution in 2025
news.text:
Malta recorded the highest annual increase in the Travel and Tourism sector’s contribution to GDP among European economies in 2025, according to the latest research by the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC).

The contribution grew by 16.8% compared to the European average of 2.6%, with data also showing that the European tourism industry is projected to grow 2.5% in 2026. 

Despite geopolitical and economic uncertainty, WTTC forecasts global Travel & Tourism growth of 2.5% in 2026, ahead of the broader economy. Europe is expected to grow faster: international visitor spending by 5.8%, leisure travel spending by 3.1%, and business travel spending by 4.2%.

The sector is expected to contribute $4.9 billion to Malta’s economy, accounting for 16.9% of GDP and supporting more than one in five jobs.

At the Summit, more than 100 speakers will discuss topics such as investment, connectivity, innovation, artificial intelligence, skills and the workforce, destination competitiveness, and sustainability.

Speaking at the opening of the summit on Wednesday, Minister for Tourism Jo Etienne Abela said the Summit offers Malta, alongside international leaders, an opportunity to discuss concrete solutions to the sector's realities, including the need for increased investment, improved connectivity, technological innovation, skills development, and sustainable growth.

He reiterated that for Malta, hosting the WTTC Global Summit is more than just an international conference. “It is an opportunity for the country to showcase its progress, share its vision for the future, and further strengthen ties with leaders and organisations shaping the future of the global tourism industry.”

He highlighted that hosting the WTTC Global Summit recognises Malta’s standing as a world-class tourist destination.

“Today, Malta is not simply welcoming the tourism world; it is serving as a platform where the sector’s future direction is being discussed,” he concluded.

WTTC Chairman Manfredi Lefebvre said Malta is an ideal host for the Summit because of its commitment to the sector, while emphasising the importance of international leaders strengthening collaboration and creating new initiatives that continue to drive growth, investment, and opportunities.
news.summary: World Travel and Tourism Council data also shows that despite geopolitical and economic uncertainty, european tourism is projected to grow by 2.5% in 2026
news.author: Juliana Zammit

news.title: Man granted bail over Marsa hit-and-run which left pedestrian grievously injured
news.text:
A 41-year-old man has been granted bail after being charged over a hit-and-run in Marsa which left a pedestrian grievously injured.

Justin Vella pleaded not guilty to 12 charges, including grievously injuring the pedestrian, speeding, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, refusing a breathalyser test, committing a number of traffic violations and leaving the scene without assisting the victim.

The court heard that Vella allegedly ran a red light before hitting the 41-year-old Bangladeshi pedestrian on Triq Diċembru 13.

Prosecutors said eyewitnesses reported that the driver did not simply flee after the collision, but later returned to the scene.

He allegedly got out of the vehicle before getting back in and speeding away once again while police officers were already at the scene.

A medical team treated the pedestrian at the scene before he was taken by ambulance to Mater Dei Hospital, where his injuries were certified as grievous.

The incident occurred at around 10pm on 20 September. Police investigations, aided by recorded footage and eyewitness accounts, eventually led officers to a BMW parked in Marsaskala, where Vella was arrested. Police said the vehicle had lost a side mirror in the collision, which was recovered from the scene.

Vella was initially denied bail when he was arraigned before Magistrate Donatella Frendo Dimech, after the prosecution raised concerns over the nature of the alleged incident and the risk of evidence being tampered with while key witnesses had yet to testify.

However, on Wednesday morning, the case was heard before Judge Neville Camilleri in the Criminal Court, who granted Vella bail against a €5,000 deposit and a €10,000 personal guarantee.

He was also placed under a daily curfew and ordered to sign the police bail book every day.

Inspector Clive Abela prosecuted.

Lawyers Amadeus Cachia and Ishmael Psaila appeared for Vella, while lawyer Michele Cardinali represented the victim.

Judge Neville Camilleri presided over the Criminal Court.
news.summary: Court hears how accused ran a red light and struck a pedestrian before returning to the scene and speeding past police
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: Man remanded in custody after allegedly harassing ex-partner, spitting in her face
news.text:
A man has been remanded in custody after pleading not guilty to a string of 15 charges involving the alleged harassment and threatening of his former partner, as well as breaches of a protection order and bail conditions.

The Albanian national, who resides in Marsaskala and works in construction, pleaded not guilty to the charges brought against him.

The court heard that the police Domestic Violence Unit had received three reports from the accused’s former partner, with whom he has an 11-month-old child. A danger assessment carried out in connection with the reports classified the situation as high risk.

The accused had previously been arraigned on 5 April and granted bail, with a protection order also issued in favour of his former partner. Under the conditions imposed by the court, communication with the woman was restricted to matters concerning their child.

However, the prosecution told the court that three further reports were subsequently filed against him in less than five weeks.

The reports allegedly involved repeated insults and threats, with the prosecution maintaining that communication between the former couple had gone beyond simply discussing their child.

In one alleged incident, the accused asked to see his son in a threatening manner. He is also accused of spitting in his former partner’s face and kicking the passenger door of a vehicle.

The charges also concern repeated calls and electronic communications allegedly made to the woman.

The man is accused of harassing his former partner and causing her to fear that violence would be used against her or her property. He is also charged with breaching the protection order issued in April, threatening or insulting her and making improper use of electronic communications.

Separate charges relate to incidents allegedly occurring in Marsaskala on 27 August and 28 September.

In relation to the August incident, the accused is charged with disturbing the public peace and threatening his former partner with stones or other hard objects, which he allegedly threw towards her vehicle.

He is also accused of disturbing the public peace during the September incident and of throwing filth at the woman.

The prosecution further alleged that the accused had failed to sign his bail book for around four months.

The court was told that police had instructed him on several occasions to attend the police station or Domestic Violence Hub, but that he allegedly failed to comply.

Police eventually located and arrested him on 5 October. The court heard that he allegedly resisted officers, refused to wear handcuffs and shouted during his arrest.

The accused also refused legal assistance when questioned by police and allegedly threw a declaration relating to legal representation onto the floor rather than signing it.

His sister had also suggested a lawyer who could represent him, but he refused.

The man maintained this position during Wednesday’s arraignment, initially telling the court that he did not want to be legally represented because he did not trust anyone to represent him and wanted additional time to find a lawyer.

The court explained that the arraignment had to proceed in accordance with procedure. Legal aid lawyer Martina Herrera represented him during the sitting.

The prosecution also charged the man with breaching the bail conditions imposed in April by allegedly committing further voluntary offences while on bail.

It requested that, in the event of a conviction, his bail be revoked and the €4,000 personal guarantee imposed by the court be forfeited in favour of the government.

Bail denied

A request for bail was made during the sitting.

The prosecution objected, arguing that important witnesses had yet to testify and expressing concern that the accused could not be trusted to observe further bail conditions.

It pointed in particular to his alleged failure to sign the bail book for four months and argued that an existing protection order had allegedly been breached three times in less than five weeks.

The defence stressed the accused remained presumed innocent and had his own version of events.

It argued that he lived separately from the alleged victim, had a stable job and could be subjected to stringent bail conditions and a protection order.

The accused also addressed the court himself, claiming that his former partner spoke to him in the same manner that he spoke to her and arguing that it was unfair that only he was facing prosecution.

After considering the nature of the accusations and the submissions made by the parties, the court denied bail and remanded the accused in custody.

The prosecution was led by Inspector Audrey Micallef. The accused was represented by legal aid lawyer Martina Herrera.

Magistrate Ingrid Bianco presided over the sitting.
news.summary: Prosecution tells court three reports were filed by man’s former partner in less than five weeks, despite an existing protection order
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as Putin marks 74th birthday
news.text:
Russia destroyed an apartment block in northern Ukraine as a birthday “gift” to Vladimir Putin, Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday, after overnight missile and drone strikes killed at least 12 people across the country, according to Ukrainian officials.

“Today, as a birthday ‘gift’ to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region,” the Ukrainian president wrote on social media. Putin turned 74 on Wednesday.

Nine people, including three children, were killed and 34 wounded when a missile hit the five-storey building, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.

“There may still be people under the rubble,” Zelensky said. “First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person.”

He said strikes also killed people in Kremenchuk and Oleksandriya and damaged apartment buildings in Dnipro.

Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed it had carried out a massive overnight strike on industrial facilities involved in producing and storing missiles and drones, as well as port and ship repair facilities in the Odesa region. It made no mention of civilian casualties.

In Kyiv, two people died in a fire caused by the attack in the city’s densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko.

Zelensky described the assault as “one of the most vile strikes” of the nearly five-year conflict. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said.

‘State of fear’

Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight at regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Poltava. It said it intercepted five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles and more than 100 drones.

Zelensky said ballistic missiles were “the greatest challenge” and that new air defences were “a vital necessity”.

He had warned the public on Tuesday night that Russia was preparing a “massive” strike, particularly on energy infrastructure. Kyiv residents spent the night in subway stations with sleeping mats and blankets.

“The whole of Kyiv is in a state of fear,” Iryna Rybalchenko, a bank worker sheltering on a platform, told AFP.

Attacks on the capital have intensified in recent weeks as winter approaches. Scheduled power cuts were introduced on Tuesday to ease pressure on the battered grid, and Klitschko warned last week that the enemy was “tearing Kyiv apart” with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.

news.title: Suspect remanded in custody after plane arrest over St Julian’s knife attack
news.text:
Updated at 2:30pm with court developments 

Florent Germain, a 25-year-old car salesman holding dual British and French citizenship, was arraigned in court on Wednesday afternoon over an attempted stabbing in St Julian’s.

The charges include attempted grievous bodily harm but causing slight bodily harm, being in the possession of a bladed weapon without having a license or permit from the Commissioner of Police, as well as breach of public peace.

The case dates back to 1 October at around 3pm, when police received an emergency report of a stabbing in Wilġa Street, St Julian’s. Emergency medical assistance was immediately dispatched to the scene, where the victim was found suffering from stab wounds to his lower back in the kidney area.

Investigators immediately secured and analysed extensive CCTV footage from surrounding properties. Due to the high density of security cameras in the area and clear daylight conditions, police were able to view full, clear footage of the entire incident.

Footage revealed that the accused was operating a rental vehicle, which police traced directly to the suspect.

A magisterial inquiry was launched and an arrest warrant was issued. The court heard that when police followed up on the address provided to the car rental company, they discovered that while the address existed, the suspect did not actually reside there.

To prevent the suspect from fleeing the island, police issued alerts. An alert was triggered on Tuesday morning at 8:30am when the suspect boarded a flight bound for London. Officers moved in immediately, arresting the man on board the aircraft.

The court was informed that the alleged victim has since been arrested for drug possession and is currently remanded in custody.

Germain pleaded not guilty to the charges.

No request for bail was made as the accused lacks a fixed address. Nonetheless, the prosecution requested a protection order for the victim and recommended that the two men be kept in separate prison divisions.

Duty Magistrate Ingrid Bianco accepted both requests.

AG lawyer Joseph Camilleri Azarov prosecuted, together with Inspectors Wayne Camilleri, Pierguido Saliba and Christian Xuereb.

Lawyers Franco Debono, Marion Camilleri and Eman Scicluna represented Germain.
news.summary: Man holding dual British-French citizenship arrested while on plane at Malta International Airport after investigations lead to him as prime suspect in St Julian’s knife attack
news.author: Karl Azzopardi

news.title: Man arrested at airport after St Julian’s stabbing
news.text:
A 25-year-old French man has been arrested at Malta International Airport following several days of investigations into the alleged stabbing of another man in Triq il-Wilġa, St Julian’s.

The incident happened on Thursday 1 October, at about 3 pm, when police were informed an ambulance had been called after a 22-year-old Englishman suffered minor injuries, allegedly caused by a sharp and pointed weapon.

Police investigations and an analysis of CCTV footage showed that, while the victim was walking, another person got out of a vehicle, approached him and then fled the scene.

Investigations continued and, early Tuesday morning, police arrested the alleged attacker as he was about to board a flight to England.

During a search of his luggage, police seized clothing which matched that seen in CCTV footage of the alleged assault.

The man remains in police custody and is expected to appear in court later today at noon.
news.summary: 25-year-old man arrested at Malta International Airport following several days of investigations into the alleged stabbing of another man in Triq il-Wilġa, St Julian’s
news.author: Karl Azzopardi

news.title: MEPs Want Employers Held Responsible for Workers’ Mental, Physical Health
news.text:
The European Parliament voted Tuesday to urge the European Commission to propose new EU rules aimed at preventing, eliminating or reducing workplace risks that can cause stress, burnout, and mental and physical disorders.

Lawmakers adopted the non-binding legislative initiative report by a vote of 413-210, with 29 abstentions. They said any proposal should be preceded by an impact assessment that includes a review of existing legislation.

Members want employers to be obligated to protect workers’ mental and physical health and ensure safe, dignified working conditions. They also want the Commission and EU countries to explicitly recognize that work-related psychosocial risks can cause occupational diseases.

Violence and harassment

Employers should adopt and carry out policies that define and prohibit violence, harassment, bullying and discriminatory behavior that undermines workers’ dignity or health, lawmakers said. They also called for early detection mechanisms and risk-based prevention protocols for violence by third parties, along with timely support for affected workers.

Risk assessments

Lawmakers recommended that employers regularly assess psychosocial risks, such as excessive workload and high work intensity, and adopt action plans with concrete measures.

They said major restructuring should be subject to a prior risk assessment conducted with workers and their representatives. Examples include teleworking arrangements and the introduction of automated decision-making and monitoring systems.

Employers should ensure that algorithmic management systems do not impose excessive burdens or monitoring on workers, and human oversight must always be maintained, lawmakers said. They also reiterated that workers have a right to disconnect from work.

Returning to work

Workers who have been absent because of psychosocial risks should have a right to a supported and sustainable return, according to the report. Lawmakers recommended that employers create individual return-to-work plans that could include adjustments to working time or work organization and changes to a worker’s tasks or workload.

“Europe must move away from a ‘burnout society’ and help create healthy workplaces where everyone can thrive, especially as the use of digital technologies and AI in the workplace continues to grow,” said Estelle Ceulemans, a Belgian lawmaker with the S&D group who wrote the report. She said the issue also affects public finances “as the cost to society is skyrocketing.”

The Commission has three months to respond. It must either tell Parliament what steps it plans to take or explain why it is refusing to propose legislation along the lines Parliament requested.

news.title: Man jailed 26 months after stealing mothers car
news.text:
A 23-year-old man has been jailed for 26 months after stealing his mother’s car and leaving her on the ground outside a police station in Birżebbuġa.

Luke Cremona was sentenced after being found guilty of a number of charges arising from a series of incidents in June 2024.

The court heard how, on 19 June 2024, Cremona was travelling with his mother and his girlfriend when an argument broke out between him and the latter.

His mother told the court that Cremona had been under the influence of drugs and alcohol at the time.

After driving to Birżebbuġa, she headed towards the police station as the argument continued. Cremona got out of the vehicle and approached his girlfriend, prompting his mother to also leave the car and attempt to make her way towards the police station while carrying her handbag and car keys.

She testified that her son pushed her from behind, causing her to fall face-first onto the ground.

Cremona then took the keys to her Peugeot 107, which also included keys to her home and apartment block, and drove away.

Members of the public alerted police after seeing the woman on the ground. Officers arrived at the scene, but Cremona had already driven away.

The vehicle was discovered abandoned later that evening in Triq il-Biċċerija, Marsa.

CCTV footage showed two people inside the car arguing shortly after it was parked, with the driver later seen damaging a side mirror. A woman was then seen leaving the vehicle.

The car was subsequently examined by forensic officers, who documented damage to the driver’s side mirror and reddish stains on the vehicle.

Cremona’s mother later told the court that the damage to the car was so extensive that a mechanic advised her it was not worth repairing. She estimated the repairs at around €3,000.

Incident at mother’s home a day earlier

The court also heard that the incident came just one day after Cremona had caused extensive damage inside his mother’s Żurrieq home.

Police had been called to the residence on 18 June following reports of a disturbance.

When Cremona’s mother arrived and allowed officers inside, they found several damaged items, including a television, vacuum cleaner, furniture, a cat scratching pole, rug and other household objects. The damage amounted to €2,485.

Cremona was arrested but was granted police bail the following morning so that he could attend a scheduled meeting with his probation officer.

During a subsequent home visit, probation officer Maryrose Farrugia testified that Cremona was highly agitated and took out a pipe used to consume cocaine, prompting her to immediately terminate the meeting.

Cremona later suggested to his mother that he would pay for the television he had damaged and the two left the house together, eventually leading to the incident in Birżebbuġa.

Cremona admitted to drug problems

During his police statement, Cremona admitted having a drug problem but repeatedly denied assaulting his mother or taking her keys.

“I never touched my mother, and I will never touch my mother,” he told investigators.

However, when he later chose to testify during the proceedings, his version of events changed several times.

He admitted taking and driving the car but initially claimed he had taken the keys from his mother’s handbag at home.

Later, after being confronted with evidence about the Birżebbuġa incident, he said the keys had been left in the ignition and that he drove off after his mother got out of the car.

The court highlighted several inconsistencies in his testimony, with the magistrate at one stage telling him: “Everyone is reminding you, except you.”

Cremona eventually admitted that he had been under the influence of both drugs and alcohol on the day and that he had damaged the car’s side mirror.

He also admitted, after being pressed by the prosecution and the court, that he had driven to Marsa to purchase drugs.

The court described Cremona as an unreliable witness, pointing to the numerous contradictions between his police statement, his testimony and the other evidence before it.

Court rejects argument that taking car was not theft

The defence argued that Cremona’s actions should not amount to theft, but rather the arbitrary exercise of a pretended right.

The court rejected this argument, finding no evidence that Cremona believed he had any right over his mother’s vehicle.

It noted that it was actually Cremona who owed his mother money for the damage he had caused, rather than the other way around.

Although there was no evidence that Cremona intended to sell the vehicle or obtain a financial profit from it, the court explained that the gain required for theft does not necessarily have to be monetary. The benefit he obtained from taking and using the vehicle was sufficient to establish the necessary intention for theft, the court said.

It also rejected the possibility that the case amounted merely to temporary unauthorised use of the car, noting that Cremona did not return it but instead abandoned it in Marsa after damaging it.

The court therefore found the theft charge proven, although it ruled that one of the alleged aggravating factors, theft by means, had not been established because the keys used were not false keys.

Mother asked court to drop case

During proceedings in March 2026, Cremona’s mother told the court that she had forgiven her son and wanted the criminal proceedings against him to stop.

She said they had resolved their differences and that Cremona had reimbursed her for the damage, including €3,000 for the car.

She also told the court that she believed her son regretted what he had done and would not have behaved in that way had he not been under the influence of drugs.

The court, however, explained that her decision could only affect offences which depended on a complaint from the injured party.

Several of the charges, including theft, causing fear of violence and criminal damage, could continue regardless of whether Cremona’s mother wished to pursue the case.

The court consequently acquitted Cremona of the charges of slightly injuring, insulting and assaulting his mother.

Court orders investigation after courtroom admission

The judgment also recounts an unusual exchange which took place while Cremona’s mother was giving evidence.

She told the court that while her son was in prison, he had offered to allow her to withdraw money from his bank account.

Cremona then interrupted her testimony from the dock, saying: “If you don’t testify, I’ll give you the money.”

When the magistrate questioned what he had just said, Cremona confirmed: “That’s what I told her.”

The magistrate immediately ordered the matter to be investigated.

Rehabilitation efforts considered

In determining punishment, the court took into account Cremona’s efforts to address his drug addiction.

His probation officer testified that he had shown a willingness to undergo rehabilitation, while a psychologist who had been following him in prison said he had cooperated and attended sessions aimed at helping him deal with difficult situations without resorting to drugs or gambling.

Caritas representatives also told the court that Cremona had expressed an interest in entering a residential rehabilitation programme.

However, the court also heard that Cremona had received 10 disciplinary reports while in prison since July 2025, including for disobeying officers, fighting and possessing prohibited items.

The court also considered his criminal record, noting that he had previously been convicted of similar offences and had failed to learn from opportunities previously given to him to avoid imprisonment.

26 months in prison

The court ultimately acquitted Cremona of six of the 12 charges against him. He was also cleared of two charges relating to breaching bail conditions after the prosecution failed to exhibit the relevant bail decree, as well as a charge of breaching a protection order after the court found that the evidence did not establish the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

Cremona was nevertheless found guilty of the remaining charges, including aggravated theft of his mother’s vehicle, causing her to fear violence, criminal damage to the vehicle and her home, driving without insurance and failing to comply with police bail.

He was sentenced to 26 months in prison, from which any time already spent in preventive custody in connection with the case is to be deducted.

The court also disqualified Cremona from holding or obtaining a driving licence for 12 months.

Magistrate Donatella Frendo Dimech presided over the court.
news.summary: A 23-year-old man is found guilty of stealing his mother’s car, causing her to fear violence, damaging her property and driving without insurance, despite mother asking court to drop proceedings after forgiving him
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: October 7: tensions remain high as conflict rages on
news.text:
Today, 7 October, marks three years since Hamas-led militants launched a surprise attack on Israel shortly after sunrise, firing thousands of rockets from the Gaza Strip and breaching the border fence at dozens of points.

An estimated 6,000 militants crossed into Israel by car, motorbike and paraglider, attacking Israeli communities and military positions in the south.

The assault killed around 1,200 people and saw approximately 250 others taken hostage, triggering Israel’s war in Gaza and a conflict that has since had repercussions across the Middle East.

The attack has been widely recognised as the deadliest single day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

On the third anniversary, Israelis gathered at memorials in Kfar Aza, Re’im and across the country. Moments of silence were held at 6:29 am, corresponding with the time the attacks began three years earlier.

At the same time, anti-government protesters in Tel Aviv dyed the Dizengoff Square fountain blood-red and displayed hundreds of photographs, flowers and messages.

Demonstrators also blocked major highways, displaying signs and banners describing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as “guilty” and the government’s leadership as a “complete failure”. Protesters also called for a public inquiry into the events surrounding the attack.

Hamas has said the October 7 attack was carried out in response to what it described as the ongoing Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories, the blockade of the Gaza Strip and the detention of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons, among other factors.

The impact on Palestinians has also been severe. According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, at least 74,200 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces over the past three years. Israel has rejected allegations that it is committing genocide, maintaining that its military operations constitute legitimate self-defence, according to NBC.

An estimated 1.9 million people, representing more than 90% of Gaza’s population, have been displaced. Of those, around 1.2 million are reportedly living in tents and shelters, amid increased risks of starvation and disease.

A formal ceasefire was reached around a year ago after both sides accepted US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan, raising hopes of an end to the fighting in Gaza. At the time, Malta welcomed Trump’s peace proposal, with the government backing a just peace based on a two-state solution and international law.

Although, Palestinians living in Malta welcomed the prospect of an end to the war, they criticised the plan, arguing that it favoured Israel, excluded Palestinian leadership from negotiations, and did not guarantee Palestinian statehood or equal benefits.

Despite this, hostilities have continued, with more than 1,460 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli military strikes since the ceasefire was announced.

Three years later, Gaza bears little resemblance to the territory that existed before the war. Concerns have grown that large-scale and potentially permanent displacement could become entrenched, amid questions over the absence of sufficient political and military mechanisms to prevent it.
news.summary: From protests to memorials, Isreal is forced to remember the attacks that left over 1,200 civilians dead three years ago on October 7 by Hamas, also resulting in over 74,200 Palestinian deaths since
news.author: Jade Bezzina

news.title: A five-decade journey from design to painting
news.text:
A career spanning graphic design, teaching and painting will come together in From Design to Light, a solo exhibition opening at the St John Ambulance & Rescue HQ in Valletta on Friday 16 October 2026.

The exhibition brings together work from across five decades, tracing Doranne Alden’s journey from her early training in art and professional career in graphic design to a life devoted to painting. Around 25 to 30 framed works will be on display, combining a retrospective selection with more recent paintings.

Michael Frendo will officially open the exhibition at 7.30pm on Friday 16 October. The exhibition will run from 17 to 31 October and is the first exhibition to be held at the St John Ambulance & Rescue HQ.

The title, From Design to Light, reflects two disciplines that have remained closely connected throughout the artist’s life. Although graphic design became her profession from an early age, painting was never abandoned. “I have always been a watercolourist,” Alden says. She describes painting not as something she returned to later in life, but as a constant thread running through her career.

Alden began learning art at around the age of 14 at Msida Polytechnic. At 18, she entered the world of graphic design, where she initially worked with Promotion Services and Rowland Phototypesetting before joining JPA Advertising at 21.

During her years at JPA, she worked on the original design and paste-up of Circle Magazine. She overaw its design during its first five years. She became head designer at approximately 24, before co-founding Details Design Ltd in 1990.

In 1995, Alden moved to Germany, where she taught painting and held exhibitions. Following her return to Malta in 2003, she continued teaching and exhibiting, while also developing a programme of painting activities. Since 2012, she has organised painting weekends and painting holidays in Gozo, as well as painting trips abroad, including group trips to Tuscany.

The exhibition brings together these different strands of her career, looking at the development of her work over five decades while also reflecting the places, experiences and memories that have informed her painting.

Among the works on display is the title painting, Catching Fishing Bait, Golden Bay (2026). The selection also includes paintings inspired by Malta and Gozo, alongside works drawn from places and memories accumulated over the years, including Comino Channel, Red Vespa, Mum’s Heavenly Terrace, The Orange Orchard in Buskett and Prickly Pear Delight.

The retrospective section opens with Freesia in Orange Vase, offering an entry point into a body of work that spans decades and demonstrates the continuing relationship between observation, design and the possibilities of watercolour.
news.summary: ​A career spanning graphic design, teaching and painting will come together in From Design to Light, a solo exhibition opening at the St John Ambulance & Rescue HQ in Valletta on Friday 16 October 2026
news.author: Laura Calleja

news.title: Diplomats: Deaths from Russian-linked hybrid attacks are a matter of when, not if
news.text:
Diplomats from the 27 European Union countries are privately working out how the bloc would respond to a hybrid attack that kills several people, a scenario five EU diplomats and officials told POLITICO is looking more likely.

The planning has also exposed disagreement over how big a security role the EU should play and whether its work overlaps with NATO’s, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential talks.

EU ambassadors have taken up the issue in recent weeks in a “restricted format” that bars phones and assistants. The talks intensified after an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport in August. Two diplomats said ambassadors met last Wednesday to focus on mass-casualty examples.

The EU has long discussed hybrid threats, which it and NATO define as subversive activity short of an act of war. It has a “hybrid toolbox” for responding to cyberattacks, election interference and sabotage. The EU says Russia has stepped up cyberattacks, sabotage and covert operations across the bloc since invading Ukraine.

The latest discussions have centered on sending emergency response teams, freeing up EU funds to help an affected country and deciding how EU leaders should communicate, one official said.

“We have to be prepared for something serious,” a senior EU diplomat said. A second official said casualties are “bound” to occur and that none so far was “sheer luck.”

Recent incidents include the Leipzig drone, a suspicious fire at a Polish ground station that handles Starlink communications and a plot to plant incendiary devices at transport hubs in the EU and U.K. Bulgarian officials said Tuesday that several sailors were missing after drones sank their ship in the Black Sea.

Teija Tiilikainen, director of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, said Russia is using increasingly lethal tools and that deaths will eventually follow. A NATO diplomat said the death of an allied citizen would put heavy pressure on both organizations to act.

Some capitals say the EU is overstepping and duplicating NATO. Oana Lungescu, a former NATO spokesperson now at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that overlap could slow decisions. Several diplomats also cited the EU’s lack of secure communications and fears of leaks, including reports that Hungary’s former foreign minister relayed leader-level talks to his Russian counterpart. A diplomat from an eastern flank country said sensitive intelligence is kept out of EU settings for that reason.

The debate coincides with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s push for an “emergency security protocol” and a “European Security Council.” Two diplomats said both are expected in a European Security Strategy due in early November. Several diplomats said the measures would take months to set up and duplicate existing tools, such as the Integrated Political Response mechanism.

Under that mechanism, the rotating EU presidency can call emergency meetings at an affected country’s request. France invoked the EU’s mutual assistance clause, Article 42.7, after the 2015 Bataclan attacks, the only time it has been used. Lungescu called that a political decision that produced little beyond coordinated investigations.

She said NATO should handle intelligence-sharing and military deterrence while the EU focuses on civilian response. She added that Russian President Vladimir Putin does not distinguish between the two organizations.

Read more via Politico
news.summary: Diplomats from the 27 European Union countries are privately working out how the bloc would respond to a hybrid attack that kills several people, a scenario five EU diplomats and officials told POLITICO is looking more likely. The planning has also exposed disagreement over how big a security role the EU should play and whether […]

news.title: Israelis mark three years since Hamas attack that set off Gaza assault
news.text:
Israelis will on Wednesday mark three years since Hamas attacked Israel on ​October 7, 2023, triggering a military assault that destroyed much of Gaza, where conditions remain dire despite a year-old ceasefire that is ‌meant to halt the war for good.

The attacks, during which militants killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages to Gaza, marked the deadliest day in Israel’s history. Israel’s subsequent bombardment and ground operations have killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza, health authorities there say.

On Wednesday, Israelis will hold a vigil at the site of the Nova music ​festival near the Gaza border, where 348 young people were killed by militants during the attack.

They will also hold an event commemorating ​the anniversary at Hostage Square in Tel Aviv.

ISRAELI ELECTION 20 DAYS AWAY

The anniversary is the first for Israelis without ⁠any hostages still held in Gaza, with those dead and alive exchanged in swaps with Hamas for Palestinians held in Israeli jails. The remains ​of the last Israeli hostage were recovered in January.

It also comes just 20 days ahead of Israel’s first election since the attack, a vote ​that is viewed as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure in power.

Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. That has frustrated many in Israel, including families of those killed in the attacks, some of whom have joined the election race.

Item 1 of 5 A woman visits the site of the Nova music festival, where partygoers were killed and kidnapped during the deadly Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, on the third anniversary of the attack, near Reim, southern Israel, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun

[1/5]A woman visits the site of the Nova music festival, where partygoers were killed and kidnapped during the deadly Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, on the third anniversary of the attack, near Reim, southern Israel, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

A poll by the Israel Democracy Institute showed ​that 68% of Jewish Israelis said that the events of October 7 were a very central or fairly central element in their decision of ​which party to vote for.

Election polls show neither Netanyahu nor his main competitors would muster enough seats in parliament to form a coalition if a vote were ‌held today.

US-BACKED ⁠CEASEFIRE FAILS TO HALT ISRAELI ATTACKS, DISARM HAMAS

The anniversary is also the first since an October 10, 2025, US-brokered ceasefire deal that halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks in Gaza or secure the disarmament of Hamas and other militant groups.

The deal left Israel in control of some 53% of Gaza, since expanded by Israeli forces to nearly two-thirds. Hamas controls the remaining third, where the 2 million population mostly live in makeshift tents ​and bombed out buildings.

US President Donald ​Trump’s so-called “Board of Peace” has proposed ⁠several plans that would see Gaza rebuilt. But those plans, which fail to account for the property rights of Palestinians whose homes were destroyed, have failed to gain the buy-in of Israel or Hamas, which are ​still deadlocked in ceasefire talks.

The two have yet to agree on the terms of a deal that would ​see Hamas lay down ⁠its weapons in exchange for Israeli troop withdrawals. Israel says it will not pull back until Hamas fully disarms; Hamas says it has agreed to a phased process but will not disarm so long as Israeli attacks continue.

Israel has kept up a bombing campaign in Gaza that has killed a number of ⁠Hamas militants ​in recent months but has also killed many civilians, say Gaza health authorities, whose ​death figures do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, the health authorities say. During the same time, five ​Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants or in combat, the military says.

Source: Reuters
news.summary: Israelis will on Wednesday mark three years since Hamas attacked Israel on ​October 7, 2023, triggering a military assault that destroyed much of Gaza, where conditions remain dire despite a year-old ceasefire that is ‌meant to halt the war for good. The attacks, during which militants killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages to Gaza, […]

news.title: Objecting to the use of the penthouse roof. Check your contract first!
news.text:
In a recent case decided by Judge Aaron Bugeja, the Civil Court had to determine the right of use of a penthouse roof to install a water tank, a water pump, airconditioning compressor and solar panels.

These matters are normally spelled out in the deed of acquisition but notwithstanding the penthouse owner insisted no use could be made of the roof of his penthouse to install a water tank and pump, an AC compressor and photovoltaic panels.

There was no dispute as to ownership of the penthouse roof. It belonged to the owner of the penthouse. What was at issue was whether the plaintiff had exclusive use of the said roof and so absolute control over what takes place on it, or whether the deed of acquisition placed any limitation on the use of the roof by the owner in the form of servitudes in favour of the underlying apartments.

In its judgment the court observed that the plaintiff’s deed of acquisition explained clearly the division of real rights, which the original vendors—the developers of the block—had drawn up. Once such deed outlines the burdens and restrictions of use. By signing such a deed, the plaintiff was expressly consenting to a restriction of use on his roof. Furthermore, the deed of acquisition was supplemented with a plan, which outlined the manner in which the roof was divided for this use. Therefore, when the original vendor sold the remaining units, he was not creating any new rights but rather allocating to the beneficiary the right of use already specified in the deed of acquisition of the plaintiff.

The court pointed out that the plaintiff had given a very partial reading of the deed of acquisition of his penthouse. The deed expressly stated that the deed incorporates the contract as well as all documents annexed to it. On this basis, the court gave weight to the plan of the roof attached to the deed. The plan outlined which apartment had exclusive use of which area on the roof. The court concluded that acceptance of the plan by the penthouse owner signalled his acceptance that he did not have absolute use of the roof.

The judgment states that there is a difference between the right to property and the right of use of the roof of the same property. The latter in legal jargon is known as the jus utendi, and in this case it was not absolute to the owner of the penthouse. The right of use of the penthouse owner in this case was limited to one area while other areas were allocated to other apartments including to the owner of the penthouse.

The fact that the penthouse or apartment was not yet in a complete state does not mean that the parties could not create, reserve or regulate real rights, easements or restrictions on the basis of plans and conditions integrated into the contracts. Contract law does not prohibit a future property, airspace or shell form from being transferred with clear conditions as to its future use. The court referred to the legal principle pacta sunt servanda, found in Article 992 of the Maltese Civil Code. It means that a contract legally entered into shall have the force of law for the contracting parties, and the parties may only depart from the obligations entered into if there is a revocation by mutual consent, or on grounds allowed by law.

The court rejected the claims by the plaintiff that there were no servitudes burdening the use of the penthouse roof and allowed the defendant—the owner of the underlying apartment—to place a water tank, a water pump, an airconditioning compressor and PV panels on the roof.

The judgment was appealed. Lawyers Paul Radmilli and Cedric Mifsud appeared for the defendant.
news.summary: In a recent case decided by Judge Aaron Bugeja, the Civil Court had to determine the right of use of a penthouse roof to install a water tank, a water pump, airconditioning compressor and solar panels
news.author: Judge Aaron Bugeja

news.title: Second block of flats approved beside medieval Dingli chapel
news.text:
The Planning Commission has approved an eight-apartment development metres away from Dingli’s medieval Santa Duminka Chapel.

This is the second development approved near the Grade 1 scheduled building despite objections over the impact on the chapel’s archaeological setting.

The application (PA/07782/24), submitted by Brian Azzopardi, involves excavation of the site, three basement garages and eight dwellings in Triq il-Kappella Medjevali. The Planning Commission voted 2-0 in favour.

The site lies within the chapel’s archaeological buffer zone. Objectors argued that the project failed to properly assess the chapel’s wider setting. Furthermore, the Dingli Local Council also objected because of the scheduled building.

The development forms part of a broader process that has opened up this previously inaccessible area of Dingli to residential construction.

Although the area was already within the development zone, construction had been hampered by the lack of road access. Infrastructure Malta constructed Triq il-Kappella Medjevali in 2021, along a road that had been schemed in local plans since the 1960s.

The road was constructed without a planning permit because it was already included in the local plans and a 2008 legal notice exempts state bodies from seeking permits for schemed roads.

Infrastructure Malta said the road was needed to provide access for fire engines and emergency services, while Moviment Graffitti, which organised protests against the road’s construction, warned it would facilitate further development around the historic chapel.

In fact, six years later the site of the new development is now separated from the chapel by the new road.

The first residential application was filed in October 2023 for a block of nine flats on an adjacent site. The Superintendent of Cultural Heritage (SCH) initially objected because of its impact on the chapel. The proposal was subsequently scaled down by removing one full floor and was eventually approved.

Azzopardi’s application was the second residential project to be proposed along the new road. When presented in November 2024, it envisaged nine flats in a five-storey block with a rooftop pool. The plans were subsequently revised to eight dwellings.

The approved project consists of three full floors and a further receded penthouse level.

The PA said the stepped design would minimise the volumes visually affecting the chapel. The SCH raised no objection to the latest plans, subject to archaeological monitoring.

The basement will contain three garages, despite the eight apartments requiring eight parking spaces. The developer will therefore pay €23,000 into the Urban Improvements Fund for the five-space shortfall.
news.summary: The Planning Commission has approved an eight-apartment development metres away from Dingli’s medieval Santa Duminka Chapel
news.author: James Debono

news.title: Only 16% expected Yorgen Fenech acquittal, MaltaToday survey finds
news.text:
Only 16.1% of people said they expected Yorgen Fenech to be acquitted, while 40.8% said they did not expect the verdict, a MaltaToday survey shows. 

Respondents were asked whether they expected Yorgen Fenech’s not-guilty verdict. They were also given the option of stating that they had not followed the case, did not know, or did not want to answer. 

Fenech was acquitted of complicity in the wilful homicide of Daphne Caruana Galizia and of associating with a person or persons for the purpose of committing a crime. A nine-member jury returned an 8-1 not-guilty verdict on both counts. 

The verdict, delivered on 2 September after a 55-day trial, came as a surprise to many and triggered public protests and expressions of disbelief and anger, including from Caruana Galizia’s family. The Attorney General has since filed an appeal against the acquittal. 

The MaltaToday survey, which included other questions that will be published on Sunday, was carried out between Tuesday 22 September and Friday 2 October 2026. The survey has a margin of error of ±3.4 percentage points. 

The findings point to a substantial level of disengagement, with 24.9% saying they had not followed the case, while a further 7.8% said they did not know what to make of the verdict and 10.5% declined to answer. 

The refusal rate is notable, suggesting that a tenth of respondents may have been reluctant to express a view on a case that remains highly sensitive and polarising, although the survey does not establish the reasons for this reluctance. 

72% of those who answered did not expect Fenech acquittal 

Among respondents, who gave one of the two substantive answers to the question (56.9%), 71.7% said they had not expected Fenech to be acquitted, while 28.3% said they had expected the verdict. 

In other words, among those who expressed a definite view, more than seven in 10 did not see the acquittal coming, compared with fewer than three in 10 who said they had expected it. These figures provide a clearer picture of expectations among respondents who were willing to express a view on the verdict. 

Majority of PL voters do not express an opinion 

A majority of PL voters did not give a definite opinion on whether they expected the not-guilty verdict. Of those who voted for the PL in the last general election, 31% said they had not followed the case, 9.7% did not know and 10.9% refused to answer. Only 13.7% said they had expected the verdict, while 34.7% said they had not. 

Among PN voters, 19.5% said they had expected the not-guilty verdict, compared with 50.9% who said they had not expected it. Only 5.3% said they did not know, while 9% refused to answer. A further 15.4% said they had not followed the case. 

Once those who had not followed the case, did not know or refused to answer are excluded, the difference between the two main parties largely disappears. Among PL voters who gave one of the two definitive answers, 71.7% said they had not expected the acquittal, compared with 28.3% who had expected it. Among PN voters who gave a definite answer, 72.2% said they had not expected the verdict, compared with 27.8% who had expected it. 

Among those who did not vote in the last election, 13.2% expected the acquittal, while 28.7% did not. The largest group in this category, 34.3%, said they had not followed the case. Another 9.8% did not know and 13.9% declined to answer. 

Small-party voters recorded a similar pattern to PN voters, with 19.6% saying they had expected the verdict and 59.2% saying they had not. Only 12.2% said they had not followed the case, while 2.6% did not know and 6.3% refused to answer. 

The figures also show a marked difference in engagement with the trial. PN voters were more likely to have followed the case and to give a definite response than PL voters or those who did not vote. 

Among PN voters, 29.6% either had not followed the case, did not know or refused to answer. The corresponding figure among PL voters was 51.7%, meaning that more than half of those who had voted Labour in the last election did not provide a definite answer. Among those who did not vote, the figure was even higher, at 58%. 

This difference in engagement helps explain why the raw figures show a wider gap between PN and PL voters. PN voters were considerably more likely to have followed the case and provide a definite response. 

Women less keen on trial 

There was little difference between men and women in expectations of the verdict. 

16.7% of men said they had expected the acquittal, compared with 15.4% of women. 

However, women were substantially more likely to say they had not followed the case—28.9% compared with 20.9% of men. 

The proportion saying, they had not expected the verdict was also higher among men, at 44.6%, than among women, at 37%. 

There was virtually no difference in refusal rates, with 10.5% of women and 10.4% of men declining to answer. 

29% of younger respondents did not follow the case 

The 36–50 age group was the most likely to say it had expected the acquittal, at 21.4%. 

This was followed by those aged 51–65 at 16.3%, while 14.9% of those aged 16–35 and 12% of those over 65 said they had expected the verdict. 

The youngest group had the highest proportion saying they had not followed the case, at 29%, while the figure among those aged 36–50 was 19.9%. 

Respondents over 65 were the least likely to say they had expected the verdict and the most likely age group to answer “don't know”, at 9.6%. 

Regional differences 

There were also differences between regions. The Southern Harbour, traditionally a strong Labour region, recorded the highest proportion expecting the acquittal of the business tycoon, at 18.6%, followed by the Western region at 18%, Northern Harbour at 17.2%, Gozo at 16.5%, Northern at 14.2% and the South Eastern region at 11.3%, the lowest figure among all regions. 

In contrast, the Northern region stood out for the proportion saying they had not expected the verdict, at 50.1%, followed by Northern Harbour at 47.4%, South Eastern at 40.2%, Gozo at 36.8%, Western at 34.3% and Southern Harbour at 30.8%. 

But the survey suggests a divergence in reactions to the verdict between the two Labour-leaning southern regions. 

In the South Eastern region, only 11.3% said they had expected the acquittal, while 40.2% said they had not expected it, almost four times as many. By contrast, in the Southern Harbour, 18.6% expected the verdict and 30.8% did not. The difference suggests that respondents in the South Eastern region were considerably more likely to say the verdict had surprised them. 

The South Eastern region also had a relatively high proportion who said they had not followed the case, at 29.2%, second only to the Southern Harbour at 30.1%. A further 8.1% said they did not know and 11.2% declined to answer. 

In all, 48.5% of respondents in the South Eastern region either had not followed the case, did not know or refused to answer. 

Gozo recorded 16.5% who expected the acquittal, while 36.8% said they had not expected it. However, 21.3% said they had not followed the case, while 9.4% did not know and 16% declined to answer, the highest refusal rate among all regions. 

Verdict surprised more than it didn’t 

Overall, the survey shows that the acquittal was substantially more likely to have been unexpected than expected among those who engaged with the question. 

But the findings also point to a second feature of public reaction—a sizeable proportion either did not follow the case, did not know how to answer or chose not to express a view. 

The 10.5% refusal rate, in particular, suggests that for some reason a significant minority were reluctant to talk about their expectations of the Fenech verdict.
news.summary: MaltaToday survey: 16.1% expected not-guilty verdict, 40.8% did not expect it, 7.8% do not know, 24.9% did not follow case and 10.5% declined to answer
